Effects of Sleep Extension on Athletic Performance—Mah et al
As with most sports, an athlete’s mental approach is crucial 
for both training and competition. With an increase in total sleep 
time, subjects reported an improved self-perception of perfor­
mance during practices and games. Subject testimonials corrob­
orated these rating scores and suggested a subjective quicker 
physical recovery, improved weight training and conditioning, 
and fewer injuries. These findings suggest that obtaining ex­
tra sleep likely has beneficial effects on overall well-being and 
the mental approach to athletics. Further research can examine 
these findings in more detail.
A common assumption in most sports is that athletes become 
increasingly tired and fatigued throughout a season. Whether 
or not this is true, this study, by showing that sleep extension 
lowers POMS fatigue scores and improves POMS vigor rat­
ings, indicates that these assumed negative mood changes can 
be avoided. Sleep extension may also contribute to athletic per­
formance by minimizing the assumed cumulative effects of a 
lengthy season and limiting an athlete’s perception of tiredness 
and fatigue. Additional sleep time improved mood even over 
the course of a competitive season. These results are consistent 
with the Kamdar et al. study8 that also noted mood improve­
ments in the POMS fatigue and vigor subscales in undergradu­
ate students following sleep extension for several weeks.
In summary, the traditional focus of both off-season and 
in-season training has been on daily training, conditioning, 
weight lifting, nutrition, and coaching. This was likewise the 
case for this study’s subjects who attested they were already 
at their peak performance prior to starting the study, since they 
had just completed their pre-season training and were begin­
ning regular season competition. However, after experiencing 
improvements in physical performance and mood following 
sleep extension, subjects acknowledged that they had previ­
ously misperceived the amount of sleep required to perform at 
their peak both physically and mentally. Thus, athletes should 
be better able to obtain their full athletic potential if optimal 
sleep is integrated into their daily training regimen.
While this investigation focused specifically on assess­
ing basketball athletic performance, future studies will need 
to examine additional sports and improve the measurements 
of athletic ability. In particular, the number of performance 
tests as well as their ability to accurately reflect competitive 
performance should be further addressed. The more valuable 
measures of athletic performance will be those tailored to the 
particular sport of interest and those that directly assess perfor­
mance during actual competition rather than practice.
More globally, accounting for differences between team ver­
sus individual sports is a critical consideration when examin­
ing other sports. For example, due to the heavy dependence on 
teamwork with others in sports such as basketball and football, 
it is difficult to clearly identify individual performance and a 
single player’s effect on a game’s outcome. Naturally, there are 
some sports where individual outcomes are fairly independent 
of teammates’ actions and are already recorded by traditional 
statistics, such as batting average and pitching in baseball and 
serving percentage in tennis. These sports more readily lend 
themselves to comparing performance in actual competition. 
Furthermore, sports that are solely dependent on the individual, 
such as swimming and track and field, more easily compare 
individual competition outcomes.
faster). The improvement in sprinting after obtaining additional 
sleep is consistent with the Waterhouse et al. study that found 
a short nap following partial sleep loss improved sprint time.12 
Similarly, the improvement in PVT reaction time seen in this 
study parallels an earlier investigation that found faster reaction 
time when nocturnal sleep was extended to 10 h/night for sev­
eral days.27 On the other hand, Belenky et al.18 showed that PVT 
speed in subjects who obtained 5 and 7 h of sleep demonstrated 
no evidence of recovery after 3 consecutive 8-h nights of sleep. 
This is similar to the nonsignificant changes in cognitive perfor­
mance tests seen after 4 days of extended sleep.14 However, the 
sleep recovery and extension periods in both these studies may 
not have been of sufficient duration to reveal improvements in 
reaction time. In contrast, the present study involved a much 
longer period (5-7 weeks of sleep extension) and found a sig­
nificant increase in PVT reaction time. It is likely that a longer 
period of sleep extension is crucial to obtaining significant PVT 
and other performance improvements.
We conducted this study under the assumption that the vast 
majority of collegiate athletes carry a sizable sleep debt due to 
chronic sleep deprivation. The total nightly baseline sleep time 
during this study (6.68 h) is consistent with the findings of pre­
vious studies examining the prevalence of insufficient sleep in 
the general public.28-30 Daytime sleepiness was confirmed by the 
baseline ESS scores as well as the substantial decrease in scores 
following sleep extension. This further supports the findings of 
Roehrs et al., in which sleep extension over 6 days improved 
alertness and reduced daytime sleepiness in sleepy subjects.27 
Furthermore, Barbato et al. revealed that by extending time in 
bed to 14 h/day for 4 weeks, subjects demonstrated mood and 
energy improvements.31 The results of the current study suggest 
similar trends consistent with these earlier investigations.
It is unclear whether this period of sleep extension elimi­
nated all sleep debt. Without utilizing an MSLT, it is very dif­
ficult to determine whether objective sleepiness, and thus sleep 
debt, was completely eliminated. Nonetheless, the length of 
sleep extension in this study and the findings of decreased ESS 
scores indicative of reduced levels of daytime sleepiness sug­
gest that subjects substantially reduced their sleep debt. Future 
studies could possibly utilize longer sleep extension periods. It 
is possible that at some point athletic indices, reaction time, and 
mood scores would no longer improve.

Both daytime sleepiness and mood improved as measured by

of the day.21 Other investigations on aerobic and 
anaerobic responses during high-intensity exercise 
have further verified these time of day differences

As with most sports, an athlete’s mental approach is crucial 
for both training and competition. With an increase in total sleep 
time, subjects reported an improved self-perception of perfor­
mance during practices and games. Subject testimonials corrob­
orated these rating scores and suggested a subjective quicker 
physical recovery, improved weight training and conditioning, 
and fewer injuries. These findings suggest that obtaining ex­
tra sleep likely has beneficial effects on overall well-being and 
the mental approach to athletics. Further research can examine 
these findings in more detail.
A common assumption in most sports is that athletes become 
increasingly tired and fatigued throughout a season. Whether 
or not this is true, this study, by showing that sleep extension 
lowers POMS fatigue scores and improves POMS vigor rat­
ings, indicates that these assumed negative mood changes can 
be avoided. Sleep extension may also contribute to athletic per­
formance by minimizing the assumed cumulative effects of a 
lengthy season and limiting an athlete’s perception of tiredness 
and fatigue. Additional sleep time improved mood even over 
the course of a competitive season. These results are consistent 
with the Kamdar et al. study8 that also noted mood improve­
ments in the POMS fatigue and vigor subscales in undergradu­
ate students following sleep extension for several weeks.
In summary, the traditional focus of both off-season and 
in-season training has been on daily training, conditioning, 
weight lifting, nutrition, and coaching. This was likewise the 
case for this study’s subjects who attested they were already 
at their peak performance prior to starting the study, since they 
had just completed their pre-season training and were begin­
ning regular season competition. However, after experiencing 
improvements in physical performance and mood following 
sleep extension, subjects acknowledged that they had previ­
ously misperceived the amount of sleep required to perform at 
their peak both physically and mentally. Thus, athletes should 
be better able to obtain their full athletic potential if optimal 
sleep is integrated into their daily training regimen.
While this investigation focused specifically on assess­
ing basketball athletic performance, future studies will need 
to examine additional sports and improve the measurements 
of athletic ability. In particular, the number of performance 
tests as well as their ability to accurately reflect competitive 
performance should be further addressed. The more valuable 
measures of athletic performance will be those tailored to the 
particular sport of interest and those that directly assess perfor­
mance during actual competition rather than practice.
More globally, accounting for differences between team ver­
sus individual sports is a critical consideration when examin­
ing other sports. For example, due to the heavy dependence on 
teamwork with others in sports such as basketball and football, 
it is difficult to clearly identify individual performance and a 
single player’s effect on a game’s outcome. Naturally, there are 
some sports where individual outcomes are fairly independent 
of teammates’ actions and are already recorded by traditional 
statistics, such as batting average and pitching in baseball and 
serving percentage in tennis. These sports more readily lend 
themselves to comparing performance in actual competition. 
Furthermore, sports that are solely dependent on the individual, 
such as swimming and track and field, more easily compare 
individual competition outcomes.

Similarly, the improvement in PVT reaction time seen in this 
study parallels an earlier investigation that found faster reaction

This is similar to the nonsignificant changes in cognitive perfor­

reaction time. In contrast, the present study involved a much 
longer period (5-7 weeks of sleep extension) and found a sig­

period of sleep extension is crucial to obtaining significant PVT

majority of collegiate athletes carry a sizable sleep debt due to 
chronic sleep deprivation. The total nightly baseline sleep time 
during this study (6.68 h) is consistent with the findings of pre­

the general public.28-30 Daytime sleepiness was confirmed by the

following sleep extension. This further supports the findings of 
Roehrs et al., in which sleep extension over 6 days improved 
alertness and reduced daytime sleepiness in sleepy subjects.27 
Furthermore, Barbato et al. revealed that by extending time in 
bed to 14 h/day for 4 weeks, subjects demonstrated mood and 
energy improvements.31 The results of the current study suggest 
similar trends consistent with these earlier investigations.
It is unclear whether this period of sleep extension elimi­
nated all sleep debt. Without utilizing an MSLT, it is very dif­
ficult to determine whether objective sleepiness, and thus sleep 
debt, was completely eliminated. Nonetheless, the length of 
sleep extension in this study and the findings of decreased ESS 
scores indicative of reduced levels of daytime sleepiness sug­
gest that subjects substantially reduced their sleep debt. Future 
studies could possibly utilize longer sleep extension periods. It 
is possible that at some point athletic indices, reaction time, and

# Notes: #000 sample (pipeline test, not sent)

Page numbers are PDF pages (Zotero item 528K3FSH). Journal pages are 943-950, so PDF p.1 = p.943.

## Citation
Mah CD, Mah KE, Kezirian EJ, Dement WC (2011). The Effects of Sleep Extension on the
Athletic Performance of Collegiate Basketball Players. SLEEP 34(7):943-950.
doi:10.5665/SLEEP.1132

## Aim (p.1-2)
"extend the nocturnal sleep duration of collegiate basketball players for a number of
weeks and to examine the effects on specific indices of athletic performance as well as
the traditional measures of reaction time, daytime sleepiness, and mood" (p.1-2)

## Design and participants
- 11 healthy Stanford men's varsity basketball players, mean age 19.4 +/- 1.4 y (p.1, p.3)
- 2-4 week habitual-sleep baseline, then 5-7 week sleep extension, minimum goal 10 h in bed/night (p.1, p.2)
- In-season, over NCAA seasons 2005-2008; naps encouraged; no alcohol or caffeine (p.2)
- Travel 3-5 days, once or twice a month; nap when 10 h not possible (p.2)
- Measured after every practice: 282 ft sprint, 10 free throws, 15 three-pointers, 1-10 well-being rating (p.3)
- Also: actigraphy + sleep logs, PVT reaction time twice daily, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, POMS mood weekly (p.2-3)
- No control group: each player compared to own baseline (p.2-3, design)

## Results
- Objective (actigraphy) sleep +110.9 +/- 79.7 min/night vs baseline, P<0.001 (p.1, p.4). Rounded to +111 min on slide.
- Actigraphy 400.7 -> 507.6 min; sleep logs 470.0 -> 624.2 min (Table 2, p.4)
- Sprint 282 ft: 16.2 -> 15.5 s, P<0.001 (Table 4, p.5)
- Free throws made of 10: 7.9 -> 8.8, P<0.001 (Table 4, p.5). Paper calls this "9% improvement" (p.5)
- Three-pointers made of 15: 10.2 -> 11.6, P<0.001 (Table 4, p.5)
- Self-rating at practice 6.9 -> 8.8; at games 7.8 -> 8.8 (Table 4, p.5)
- Evening PVT mean reaction time 336.03 -> 285.91 ms (Table 3, p.4)
- Epworth sleepiness 9.64 -> 3.36; POMS fatigue 8.24 -> 1.45; vigor 11.71 -> 18.14 (Table 6, p.6)

## Limitations
- Authors: no adjustment for multiple comparisons (p.3)
- Authors: practice drills, not competition performance; need other sports and better measures (p.6)
- Authors: unclear whether all sleep debt was eliminated (p.6)
- Ours: 11 players, one team, one sport, all men; no control group, so season timing, practice effects, and expectation cannot be ruled out
- Ours: players knew the study goal (no blinding described)
- Ours: well-being and injury comments are self-report and testimonials (p.6), not measured outcomes

# Notes: #000 sample (pipeline test, not sent)

Page numbers are PDF pages (Zotero item 528K3FSH). Journal pages are 943-950, so PDF p.1 = p.943.

## Citation
Mah CD, Mah KE, Kezirian EJ, Dement WC (2011). The Effects of Sleep Extension on the
Athletic Performance of Collegiate Basketball Players. SLEEP 34(7):943-950.
doi:10.5665/SLEEP.1132

## Aim (p.1-2)
"extend the nocturnal sleep duration of collegiate basketball players for a number of
weeks and to examine the effects on specific indices of athletic performance as well as
the traditional measures of reaction time, daytime sleepiness, and mood" (p.1-2)

## Design and participants
- 11 healthy Stanford men's varsity basketball players, mean age 19.4 +/- 1.4 y (p.1, p.3)
- 2-4 week habitual-sleep baseline, then 5-7 week sleep extension, minimum goal 10 h in bed/night (p.1, p.2)
- In-season, over NCAA seasons 2005-2008; naps encouraged; no alcohol or caffeine (p.2)
- Travel 3-5 days, once or twice a month; nap when 10 h not possible (p.2)
- Measured after every practice: 282 ft sprint, 10 free throws, 15 three-pointers, 1-10 well-being rating (p.3)
- Also: actigraphy + sleep logs, PVT reaction time twice daily, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, POMS mood weekly (p.2-3)
- No control group: each player compared to own baseline (p.2-3, design)

## Results
- Objective (actigraphy) sleep +110.9 +/- 79.7 min/night vs baseline, P<0.001 (p.1, p.4). Rounded to +111 min on slide.
- Actigraphy 400.7 -> 507.6 min; sleep logs 470.0 -> 624.2 min (Table 2, p.4)
- Sprint 282 ft: 16.2 -> 15.5 s, P<0.001 (Table 4, p.5)
- Free throws made of 10: 7.9 -> 8.8, P<0.001 (Table 4, p.5). Paper calls this "9% improvement" (p.5)
- Three-pointers made of 15: 10.2 -> 11.6, P<0.001 (Table 4, p.5)
- Self-rating at practice 6.9 -> 8.8; at games 7.8 -> 8.8 (Table 4, p.5)
- Evening PVT mean reaction time 336.03 -> 285.91 ms (Table 3, p.4)
- Epworth sleepiness 9.64 -> 3.36; POMS fatigue 8.24 -> 1.45; vigor 11.71 -> 18.14 (Table 6, p.6)

## Limitations
- Authors: no adjustment for multiple comparisons (p.3)
- Authors: practice drills, not competition performance; need other sports and better measures (p.6)
- Authors: unclear whether all sleep debt was eliminated (p.6)
- Ours: 11 players, one team, one sport, all men; no control group, so season timing, practice effects, and expectation cannot be ruled out
- Ours: players knew the study goal (no blinding described)
- Ours: well-being and injury comments are self-report and testimonials (p.6), not measured outcomes

--- teams.md
**Research in 5 · #000: The Effects of Sleep Extension on the Athletic Performance of Collegiate Basketball Players**
These D1 players averaged under 7 hours a night in season. What changed when they chased 10 hours in bed?

**What did the researchers do?**
If in-season college athletes sleep a lot more for several weeks, do their sprint, shooting, reaction time, and mood change?
- Players kept their normal sleep for 2 to 4 weeks to set a baseline.
- Then for 5 to 7 weeks they aimed for at least 10 hours in bed a night, with naps encouraged.
- Sleep was tracked with wrist actigraphy and sleep logs through the regular season.
- After every practice: a timed 282 ft sprint, 10 free throws, and 15 three-pointers.

**What were the results?**
- **+111 min** more sleep per night, measured by actigraphy
- **-0.7 s** on the 282 ft sprint (16.2 to 15.5 seconds)
- **7.9→8.8** free throws made out of 10
- Three-pointers made out of 15 rose from 10.2 to 11.6 (p. 5).
- Reaction time got faster, daytime sleepiness dropped, and fatigue scores fell while vigor rose (p. 4, 6).
- Players rated how they felt at practice higher: 6.9 to 8.8 on a 10-point scale (p. 5).

**What does this mean?**
Sleep looks like a trainable performance lever, not just recovery. The size of the gains is uncertain because nothing was compared against a control group.
- **Strength and Conditioning:** Sprint times dropped in the middle of a season. Treat sleep as part of the program, not what is left over.
- **Sports Medicine:** Healthy in-season athletes started out sleepy (Epworth 9.6, down to 3.4). Screen sleep in routine check-ins.
- **Mental Health:** Fatigue, tension, and mood scores all improved. Sleep is a low-cost first step before other supports.
- **Sport Coaches:** Late film, early lifts, and travel cut into sleep. Schedule decisions are performance decisions.

**Coaching takeaways**
1. Watch sleep like training load: ask about it in check-ins and look for patterns before big weeks.
2. Pilot a 2 to 3 week sleep push with one willing team and track sprint and wellness data.
3. Plan travel days around sleep: protect nap windows when 10 hours in bed is not possible.

**How much to trust it:** Preliminary. Before and after, no control group, 11 Stanford men's basketball players. Limits: Small, single team, all men; no control group, so season timing could explain gains; practice drills, not game performance.

**Discuss:** Where does our own schedule (lifts, film, travel) cost athletes the most sleep, and what could we move?

Mah et al. (2011). The Effects of Sleep Extension on the Athletic Performance of Collegiate Basketball Players. SLEEP. https://doi.org/10.5665/SLEEP.1132

**Research in 5 · #000: The Effects of Sleep Extension on the Athletic Performance of Collegiate Basketball Players**
These D1 players averaged under 7 hours a night in season. What changed when they chased 10 hours in bed?

**What did the researchers do?**
If in-season college athletes sleep a lot more for several weeks, do their sprint, shooting, reaction time, and mood change?

- Sleep was tracked with wrist actigraphy and sleep logs through the regular season.
- After every practice: a timed 282 ft sprint, 10 free throws, and 15 three-pointers.

- **+111 min** more sleep per night, measured by actigraphy

- Players rated how they felt at practice higher: 6.9 to 8.8 on a 10-point scale (p. 5).

Sleep looks like a trainable performance lever, not just recovery. The size of the gains is uncertain because nothing was compared against a control group.

- **Mental Health:** Fatigue, tension, and mood scores all improved. Sleep is a low-cost first step before other supports.
- **Sport Coaches:** Late film, early lifts, and travel cut into sleep. Schedule decisions are performance decisions.

**Each week:** you give me a paper as a PDF, a DOI or URL, or a Zotero item. From one content file (`review.json`) the build makes:
- **The deck:** 5 slides in Baylor green/gold, exported to PDF for Teams. The slides are the paper, then your four questions (what the researchers did, the results, what it means by role, coaching takeaways), with the discussion question on the last slide.
- **A Teams post and a plain-text email** with the same headings and the "how much to trust it" rating.
- **A new row in the index:** a CSV on Drive that opens in Excel.

Because all three outputs come from the same file, the deck, post and email can't disagree on a number. Before anything is written, every number goes into a notes file with its page in the paper.

**Test run:** I built a practice review (#000, not for sending) from Mah et al. 2011, the sleep-extension study in Stanford basketball players, pulled from your Zotero library.

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. Exception: claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) ARE fetchable via your claude.ai login — use WebFetch, not curl (curl gets the SPA shell or a Cloudflare 403).
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.

                    Abstract
Background
Patellar tendinopathy is a prevalent overuse injury in sports requiring rapid force production by the knee extensors and is particularly common among elite volleyball players. This study aimed to compare lower-limb frontal-plane alignment between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball athletes.
Methods
We conducted a cross-sectional descriptive study among 22 elite male volleyball players from Alborz Province, selected through purposive sampling. We diagnosed patellar tendinopathy using the Royal London Hospital Test (RLHT). Standardized weight-bearing radiographs of the lower limbs were obtained. Seven anatomical and mechanical alignment parameters, including anatomical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (aLDFA), mechanical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (mLDFA), anatomical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (aMPTA), mechanical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (mMPTA), anatomical TibioFemoral Angle (aTFA), anatomical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (aLDTA), and mechanical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (mLDTA), were measured. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Considering the normal distribution of the data, paired t-tests were employed to compare alignment measures between affected and unaffected knees. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05, and analyses were performed using SPSS version 26.
Results
No significant differences were observed between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy (p ≥ 0.05) across any of the measured anatomical or mechanical alignment parameters, including aLDFA, mLDFA, aMPTA, mMPTA, aTFA, aLDTA, and mLDTA.
Conclusion
These findings indicate that patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball players is unlikely to be associated with static frontal-plane lower-limb alignment. Rather, functional and dynamic biomechanical factors may play a more prominent role in the onset and progression of the condition. Thus, future clinical and research efforts should prioritize training load regulation and movement pattern correction rather than relying solely on static alignment evaluations.

# Zotero — Printing Press CLI

## Prerequisites: Install the CLI

This skill drives the `zotero-research-library-pp-cli` binary. **You must verify the CLI is installed before invoking any command from this skill.** If it is missing, install it first:

1. Install via the Printing Press installer. It defaults binaries to `$HOME/.local/bin` on macOS/Linux and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\PrintingPress\bin` on Windows:
   ```bash
   npx -y @mvanhorn/printing-press-library install zotero-research-library --cli-only
   ```
2. Verify: `zotero-research-library-pp-cli --version`
3. Ensure the reported install directory is on `$PATH` for the agent/runtime that will invoke this skill.

If the `npx` install fails (no Node, offline, etc.), fall back to a direct Go install (requires Go 1.26.5 or newer). This installs into `$GOPATH/bin` (default `$HOME/go/bin`), so add that directory to `$PATH` instead:

```bash
go install github.com/mvanhorn/printing-press-library/library/productivity/zotero-research-library/cmd/zotero-research-library-pp-cli@latest
```

If `--version` reports "command not found" after install, the runtime cannot see the binary directory on `$PATH`. Do not proceed with skill commands until verification succeeds.

zotero-research-library-pp-cli mirrors your library into a local SQLite cache using the API's version cursors, then answers research-grounding questions offline: ranked full-text search with snippets, collection trees, recent-additions triage, and Better BibTeX citekey lookups. What the Web API meters at 100 items a page, your cache answers in milliseconds.

## When to Use This CLI

Use this CLI whenever a task needs the user's own research library: grounding answers in their curated corpus, finding citations, browsing collections, or exporting BibTeX. It is the substrate for research-grounding workflows — search the local cache first, fall back to live API or open web only when the cache misses.

## Anti-triggers

Do not use this CLI for:
- Do not use this CLI to create, modify, or delete items in Zotero — it is read-only against the API
- Do not use it for PDF download or attachment file retrieval; it indexes extracted text only
- Do not use it for open-web literature search — it covers the user's own library

## Unique Capabilities
Zotero CLI — scriptable access to your Zotero library via the Web API v3.

Sync your library into a local SQLite cache and import RIS bibliographies with
duplicate detection. Reads sync to the local cache for fast offline lookup;
writes go through the live API with write-token idempotency and version-aware
conflict detection.

Not yet implemented: item search/fetch/edit, PDF download, add-by-DOI, tag and
collection CRUD, and bibliography export. See README "Known Gaps".

Agent mode: add --agent to any command for JSON output and non-interactive defaults.
Health check: run 'zotero-research-library-pp-cli doctor' to verify auth and connectivity.

Usage:
  zotero-research-library-pp-cli [command]

Available Commands:
  auth        Manage Zotero API credentials
  completion  Generate the autocompletion script for the specified shell
  doctor      Diagnose configuration, auth, and connectivity
  help        Help about any command
  import      Import an RIS file into the library
  sync        Pull updates from Zotero into the local store
  version     Print version

Flags:
      --agent              Set all agent-friendly defaults (--json --compact --no-input --no-color --yes)
      --compact            Return only key fields for minimal token usage
      --config string      Config file path
      --dry-run            Show request without sending
  -h, --help               help for zotero-research-library-pp-cli
      --human-friendly     Enable colored output and rich formatting
      --json               Output as JSON
      --library string     Library to operate on: "user" or "group:<id>" (default from config)
      --no-bbt             Disable Better BibTeX JSON-RPC calls (citekey backfill)
      --no-cache           Bypass HTTP response cache
      --no-color           Disable colored output
      --no-input           Disable all interactive prompts (for CI/agents)
      --no-sync            Skip implicit sync on read commands
      --quiet              Suppress output; exit code communicates result

Import parses an RIS file and creates the records as items via the
Zotero Web API, skipping anything already present.

Duplicate detection compares each incoming record against the local store,
so run 'sync' first — an out-of-date store will re-create items you already
have. Matching is by normalised DOI and by normalised title (lowercased,
punctuation and whitespace stripped); either alone misses real duplicates,
so both run by default.

Writes carry Zotero-Write-Token, so a network-retried batch is deduplicated
server-side rather than double-creating.

Use --dry-run to see what would be created without sending any writes.

Usage:
  zotero-research-library-pp-cli import <file.ris> [flags]

Flags:
      --collection string   Add imported items to this collection (created if it does not exist)
      --dedupe string       Duplicate detection: "doi,title", "doi", "title", or "none" (default "doi,title")
  -h, --help                help for import
      --item-type string    Zotero item type for records whose RIS TY is missing or unrecognised (default "journalArticle")

This study aimed to compare lower-limb frontal-plane alignment between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball athletes. We conducted a cross-sectional descriptive study among 22 elite male volleyball players from Alborz Province, selected through purposive sampling. We diagnosed patellar tendinopathy using the Royal London Hospital Test (RLHT). Standardized weight-bearing radiographs of the lower limbs were obtained. Seven anatomical and mechanical alignment parameters, including anatomical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (aLDFA), mechanical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (mLDFA), anatomical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (aMPTA), mechanical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (mMPTA), anatomical TibioFemoral Angle (aTFA), anatomical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (aLDTA), and mechanical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (mLDTA), were measured. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Considering the normal distribution of the data, paired t-tests were employed to compare alignment measures between affected and unaffected knees. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05, and analyses were performed using SPSS version 26. No significant differences were observed between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy (p ≥ 0.05) across any of the measured anatomical or mechanical alignment parameters, including aLDFA, mLDFA, aMPTA, mMPTA, aTFA, aLDTA, and mLDTA. These findings indicate that patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball players is unlikely to be associated with static frontal-plane lower-limb alignment. Rather, functional and dynamic biomechanical factors may play a more prominent role in the onset and progression of the condition. Thus, future clinical and research efforts should prioritize training load regulation and movement pattern correction rather than relying solely on static alignment evaluations."/>

This study aimed to compare lower-limb frontal-plane alignment between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball athletes. We conducted a cross-sectional descriptive study among 22 elite male volleyball players from Alborz Province, selected through purposive sampling. We diagnosed patellar tendinopathy using the Royal London Hospital Test (RLHT). Standardized weight-bearing radiographs of the lower limbs were obtained. Seven anatomical and mechanical alignment parameters, including anatomical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (aLDFA), mechanical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (mLDFA), anatomical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (aMPTA), mechanical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (mMPTA), anatomical TibioFemoral Angle (aTFA), anatomical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (aLDTA), and mechanical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (mLDTA), were measured. These findings indicate that patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball players is unlikely to be associated with static frontal-plane lower-limb alignment. # Notes: #001 alignment and jumper's knee

Source: ABSTRACT ONLY. Published online 2026-09-12 as an early-access version
(Springer Link / BMC). Full-text HTML and PDF were not available on 2026-09-16
(PDF URL returned 404 via direct download and in Chrome). Added to Zotero by RIS
import with tag "Research in 5" (no PDF attached). Rebuild from the full text when
it posts: means, SDs, affected-knee counts, and stated limitations are not in the abstract.

## Citation
Saraee D, Piri H, Sheikhhoseini R, Hajizadeh R (2026). Comparison of lower limb
alignment in knees with and without patellar tendinopathy among elite volleyball
players: a cross-sectional study. Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research.
doi:10.1186/s13018-026-07229-w

## Aim (abstract, Background)
"compare lower-limb frontal-plane alignment between knees with and without patellar
tendinopathy in elite volleyball athletes"

## Design and participants (abstract, Methods)
- Cross-sectional descriptive study
- 22 elite male volleyball players, Alborz Province, purposive sampling
- Patellar tendinopathy diagnosed with the Royal London Hospital Test (RLHT), a clinical palpation test
- Standardized weight-bearing radiographs of the lower limbs
- 7 frontal-plane angles: aLDFA, mLDFA (distal femur), aMPTA, mMPTA (proximal tibia), aTFA (tibiofemoral), aLDTA, mLDTA (distal tibia)
- Paired t-tests comparing affected vs unaffected knees; p <= 0.05; SPSS 26
- "Compared each player's painful knee with their pain-free knee": inferred from the paired t-test between affected and unaffected knees. Confirm against full text.

## Results (abstract, Results)
- No significant differences between knees with and without PT (p >= 0.05) on any of the 7 parameters
- No means, SDs, effect sizes, or count of affected knees in the abstract

## Authors' conclusion (abstract)
- PT in elite volleyball players "is unlikely to be associated with static frontal-plane lower-limb alignment"
- "functional and dynamic biomechanical factors may play a more prominent role"
- Future work should "prioritize training load regulation and movement pattern correction rather than relying solely on static alignment evaluations"
- Note: load and movement were not measured in this study; that part is the authors' interpretation.

## Limitations
- Ours: 22 men from one region; one time point, so no cause and effect
- Ours: within-player (paired) comparison. If alignment is similar in both legs, a risk from alignment would not show up side to side. The design does not compare injured vs healthy players.
- Ours: frontal plane and static standing X-rays only; no landing mechanics, jump load, or tendon imaging
- Ours: diagnosis by clinical test (RLHT), no imaging confirmation mentioned in abstract
- Ours: null result in a small sample may miss a small real difference (no power analysis in abstract)
- Ours: review built from abstract only

Research in 5 #001 (Saraee et al. 2026) is ready to post, and the paper is now in your Zotero library. I built this review from the abstract only, because the full text isn't online yet.

**Why abstract only:** the journal put the article online on Sept 12 as an early-access version. Only the abstract is public, and the PDF link returns "not found" in plain downloads and in your Chrome browser. The abstract still covers what the review needs: 22 elite male players, 7 leg alignment angles measured on standing X-rays, and no difference on any of them between knees with and without jumper's knee. It doesn't give means, SDs or how many knees were affected. Slide 1 and both posts say the summary is based on the abstract.

**What the review says:**
- **Evidence:** Preliminary. It's a small, single-visit study of men from one region, and it compares legs within the same player rather than injured players against healthy ones.
- **Main message:** how the leg bones line up at rest didn't explain jumper's knee. The authors point to training load and movement patterns instead, which the study didn't measure, and the slides say so.
- **Takeaways:** look at jump load and landing mechanics before blaming alignment, and try simple jump counts in volleyball practice.

All 5 slides passed the visual check. I sent you the PDF, `teams.md` and `email.txt`. They're also on Drive in `Research_in_5/001_alignment-jumpers-knee/`, and the index now lists #001.

**Zotero:** added as item ZEMKG5EA with all 4 authors, the DOI and the abstract, tagged "Research in 5". No PDF is attached yet.

**Before you post:**
- **Send now or wait?** You can post now as abstract-only, or wait for the full text. When it's out, send me the PDF and I'll add the actual numbers and republish.
- **Merge PR #1** (https://github.com/erash11/Weekly_Research_Review/pull/1), which now includes this review, then run `git pull` in `DEV/Weekly_Research_Review`.
- **Check the design detail:** I read the paired statistics as comparing each player's painful knee with their other knee. That's an inference from the abstract, flagged in `notes.md`, and it drives one of the stated limits, so confirm it when the full text comes out.

  "abstract": "Patellar tendinopathy is a prevalent overuse injury in sports requiring rapid force production by the knee extensors and is particularly common among elite volleyball players. This study aimed to compare lower-limb frontal-plane alignment between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball athletes. We conducted a cross-sectional descriptive study among 22 elite male volleyball players from Alborz Province, selected through purposive sampling. We diagnosed patellar tendinopathy using the Royal London Hospital Test (RLHT). Standardized weight-bearing radiographs of the lower limbs were obtained. Seven anatomical and mechanical alignment parameters, including anatomical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (aLDFA), mechanical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (mLDFA), anatomical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (aMPTA), mechanical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (mMPTA), anatomical TibioFemoral Angle (aTFA), anatomical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (aLDTA), and mechanical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (mLDTA), were measured. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Considering the normal distribution of the data, paired t-tests were employed to compare alignment measures between affected and unaffected knees. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05, and analyses were performed using SPSS version 26. No significant differences were observed between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy (p ≥ 0.05) across any of the measured anatomical or mechanical alignment parameters, including aLDFA, mLDFA, aMPTA, mMPTA, aTFA, aLDTA, and mLDTA. These findings indicate that patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball players is unlikely to be associated with static frontal-plane lower-limb alignment. Rather, functional and dynamic biomechanical factors may play a more prominent role in the onset and progression of the condition. Thus, future clinical and research efforts should prioritize training load regulation and movement pattern correction rather than relying solely on static alignment evaluations.",

Comparison of lower limb alignment in knees with and 
without patellar tendinopathy among elite volleyball 
players: a cross-sectional study
Danial Saraee  · Hashem Piri  · Rahman Sheikhhoseini  · Razieh Hajizadeh
Received: 28 July 2026 / Accepted: 3 September 2026
© The Author(s) 2026
Abstract
Background  Patellar tendinopathy is a prevalent overuse injury in sports requiring rapid force production by the 
knee extensors and is particularly common among elite volleyball players. This study aimed to compare lower-
limb frontal-plane alignment between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball athletes.
Methods  We conducted a cross-sectional descriptive study among 22 elite male volleyball players from Alborz 
Province, selected through purposive sampling. We diagnosed patellar tendinopathy using the Royal London Hos­
pital Test (RLHT). Standardized weight-bearing radiographs of the lower limbs were obtained. Seven anatomical 
and mechanical alignment parameters, including anatomical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (aLDFA), mechanical 
Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (mLDFA), anatomical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (aMPTA), mechanical Medial 
Proximal Tibial Angle (mMPTA), anatomical TibioFemoral Angle (aTFA), anatomical Lateral Distal Tibial 
Angle (aLDTA), and mechanical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (mLDTA), were measured. Normality was assessed 
using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Considering the normal distribution of the data, paired t-tests were employed to 
compare alignment measures between affected and unaffected knees. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05, 
and analyses were performed using SPSS version 26.
Results  No significant differences were observed between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy (p ≥ 0.05) 
across any of the measured anatomical or mechanical alignment parameters, including aLDFA, mLDFA, aMPTA, 
mMPTA, aTFA, aLDTA, and mLDTA.
Conclusion  These findings indicate that patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball players is unlikely to be associ­
ated with static frontal-plane lower-limb alignment. Rather, functional and dynamic biomechanical factors may 
play a more prominent role in the onset and progression of the condition. Thus, future clinical and research efforts 
should prioritize training load regulation and movement pattern correction rather than relying solely on static 
alignment evaluations.

Introduction
Volleyball is a fast-paced sport that involves frequent jumping and repetitive overhead movements, placing sub­
stantial mechanical demands on both the upper and lower extremities. These demands expose players to a vari­
ety of acute and overuse injuries, including ankle sprains, finger and thumb sprains, shoulder overuse injuries, 
concussions, and patellar tendinopathy (PT) [1–3]. During jump-landing activities, high forces are transmitted 
through the lower-limb joints, contributing to both acute injuries, such as Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) 
tears, and overuse conditions like PT [3, 4].
PT, also known as “jumper’s knee,” is a common overuse injury resulting from excessive loading of the patel­
lar tendon. This condition develops when the tendon cannot adequately adapt to repeated mechanical demands. It 
is estimated that approximately 20% of elite basketball athletes experience PT[5]. PT is a debilitating condition 
that can lead to prolonged absence from sport and may even result in early retirement from athletic participation 
[6]. In this context, Lian et al. [7] reported the prevalence of tendinopathy among elite athletes in different sports, 
showing that it affected 44.6% of volleyball players and 31.9% of basketball players.
Furthermore, prevalence was higher among male athletes (13.5%) than female athletes (5.6%), indicating a 
greater risk in elite male athletes [7]. Tendinopathy is a complex, multifactorial tendon disorder characterized 
by pain, reduced functional capacity, and decreased load tolerance. The most common overuse tendinopathies 
include rotator cuff tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, gluteal tendinopathy, and Achilles tendinopathy [8].
Deviations from normal postural alignment can reduce mechanical efficiency and predispose individuals to 
musculoskeletal and neuromuscular injuries [9]. The lower extremity is the most common site of injury in volley­
ball, accounting for 50–60% of all reported injuries [10, 11]. Poor lower-limb alignment during the deceleration 
phase of closed kinetic chain movements, such as landing, is considered a risk factor for sports-related injuries 
in volleyball players [12].
At the professional and elite levels, the ankle accounts for the greatest proportion of lower-extremity injuries, 
representing 25.9% of all reported injuries [10]. The knee is the second most common site of acute lower-limb 
injuries in volleyball players. Advances in medical imaging have also improved the assessment and character­
ization of sports-related knee injuries, including MRI-based approaches for detailed evaluation of injured knee 
structures [13].
Additionally, the knee is the most frequent site of overuse injuries in the lower extremity among volleyball 
players [2, 10]. PT, a primary source of anterior knee pain, is typically characterized by localized pain at the 
inferior pole of the patella and load-related pain that intensifies during knee extensor activity, particularly during 
movements that require energy storage and release within the patellar tendon [7]. In this regard, Lazaro et al. [14] 
investigated patellar mobility and lower limb kinematics during functional activities in individuals with and with­
out PT. The results indicated that patients with PT exhibited increased lateral patellar mobility compared to those 
without tendinopathy. Additionally, increased hip adduction and greater external ankle rotation were also associ­
ated with PT [14]. Moreover, Khair et al. [15] investigated the modifications in landing mechanics during vertical 
jump tasks in elite volleyball players with PT. The study identified significant alterations in knee joint kinemat­
ics, indicating that PT may influence neuromuscular control and movement patterns during jump landings [15]. 
Therefore, assessing lower-limb alignment during dynamic tasks may be a potential approach for identifying 
individuals at risk for future musculoskeletal pain or injury [16]. In this regard, Shultz et al. [17] examined the 
relationship between lower-extremity alignment characteristics and anterior knee joint laxity. They demonstrated 
that the tibiofemoral angle had the greatest influence on anterior knee laxity [17].
Given the high prevalence of PT among volleyball players likely related to the repetitive jumping and land­
ing demands of the sport and the lack of studies investigating the relationship between PT and frontal-plane 
lower-limb alignment in elite volleyball athletes, the present study aimed to determine whether lower-limb align­
ment differed between affected and unaffected knees in elite male volleyball players with unilateral patellar 
tendinopathy."},{"page":3,"text":"Article in Press
Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
https://doi.org/10.1186/s13018-026-07229-w
Materials and methods
This study was reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epide­
miology (STROBE) guidelines for cross-sectional studies [18].
Participants
The present study was a cross-sectional investigation. The source population consisted of elite male volley­
ball players competing in volleyball clubs in Alborz Province, Iran. The study sample included elite male vol­
leyball players, with a mean age of 19.59 ± 2.04 years, a mean height of 191.68 ± 6.72 cm, a mean weight of 
80.59 ± 9.02 kg, and a mean Body Mass Index (BMI) of 22.24 ± 1.88. Initial screening followed the predefined 
inclusion criteria. The inclusion criteria were unilateral PT identified using the Royal London Hospital Test 
(RLHT), male sex, age 18–30 years, and provision of written informed consent. Athletes were excluded if they 
had severe spinal abnormalities identified using the New York test, a history of lower-extremity surgery, or bilat­
eral tendinopathy. Participants were recruited from volleyball clubs in Alborz Province, Iran, between [2025-05-
22] and [2025-08-23], using purposive sampling. Using G*Power for a paired-samples t-test, with an assumed 
effect size of 0.55, α = 0.05, and statistical power of 0.80 (1 − β = 0.80), the required sample size was 22 partici­
pants [19].
Procedures
PT was clinically assessed using the RLHT, which has a reported sensitivity of 88% and specificity of 98% [20]. 
The test was performed with the participant supine and the knee fully extended. The patellar tendon was palpated 
along its entire length, from the proximal to distal attachment at the inferior pole of the patella, to assess for 
localized tenderness. When tenderness was detected, the same area was palpated again, with tenderness absent 
or diminished during knee flexion, indicating PT (Fig. 1) [20]. Both knees were assessed independently using the 
RLHT. Knees demonstrating a positive test were classified as affected, whereas knees with a negative test were 
classified as unaffected.
After identifying participants with PT using the RLHT, they were referred to an Imaging Center in Karaj for 
lower limb radiography. Imaging was conducted using the Payamed system (Iran), with radiation doses adjusted 
appropriately for each region: 80 kV and 200 mA for the pelvis and femur, 65 kV and 125 mA for the knee, and 
55 kV and 100 mA for the tibia and ankle.

of tenderness with the knee

Comparison of lower limb alignment in knees with and 
without patellar tendinopathy among elite volleyball 
players: a cross-sectional study
Danial Saraee  · Hashem Piri  · Rahman Sheikhhoseini  · Razieh Hajizadeh
Received: 28 July 2026 / Accepted: 3 September 2026
© The Author(s) 2026
Abstract
Background  Patellar tendinopathy is a prevalent overuse injury in sports requiring rapid force production by the 
knee extensors and is particularly common among elite volleyball players. This study aimed to compare lower-
limb frontal-plane alignment between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball athletes.
Methods  We conducted a cross-sectional descriptive study among 22 elite male volleyball players from Alborz 
Province, selected through purposive sampling. We diagnosed patellar tendinopathy using the Royal London Hos­
pital Test (RLHT). Standardized weight-bearing radiographs of the lower limbs were obtained. Seven anatomical 
and mechanical alignment parameters, including anatomical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (aLDFA), mechanical 
Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (mLDFA), anatomical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (aMPTA), mechanical Medial 
Proximal Tibial Angle (mMPTA), anatomical TibioFemoral Angle (aTFA), anatomical Lateral Distal Tibial 
Angle (aLDTA), and mechanical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (mLDTA), were measured. Normality was assessed 
using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Considering the normal distribution of the data, paired t-tests were employed to 
compare alignment measures between affected and unaffected knees. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05, 
and analyses were performed using SPSS version 26.
Results  No significant differences were observed between knees with and without patellar tendinopathy (p ≥ 0.05) 
across any of the measured anatomical or mechanical alignment parameters, including aLDFA, mLDFA, aMPTA, 
mMPTA, aTFA, aLDTA, and mLDTA.
Conclusion  These findings indicate that patellar tendinopathy in elite volleyball players is unlikely to be associ­
ated with static frontal-plane lower-limb alignment. Rather, functional and dynamic biomechanical factors may 
play a more prominent role in the onset and progression of the condition. Thus, future clinical and research efforts 
should prioritize training load regulation and movement pattern correction rather than relying solely on static 
alignment evaluations.
Keywords  Tendinopathy · Professional athlete · Lower extremity · Radiologic angles · Injury

Introduction
Volleyball is a fast-paced sport that involves frequent jumping and repetitive overhead movements, placing sub­
stantial mechanical demands on both the upper and lower extremities. These demands expose players to a vari­
ety of acute and overuse injuries, including ankle sprains, finger and thumb sprains, shoulder overuse injuries, 
concussions, and patellar tendinopathy (PT) [1–3]. During jump-landing activities, high forces are transmitted 
through the lower-limb joints, contributing to both acute injuries, such as Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) 
tears, and overuse conditions like PT [3, 4].
PT, also known as “jumper’s knee,” is a common overuse injury resulting from excessive loading of the patel­
lar tendon. This condition develops when the tendon cannot adequately adapt to repeated mechanical demands. It 
is estimated that approximately 20% of elite basketball athletes experience PT[5]. PT is a debilitating condition 
that can lead to prolonged absence from sport and may even result in early retirement from athletic participation 
[6]. In this context, Lian et al. [7] reported the prevalence of tendinopathy among elite athletes in different sports, 
showing that it affected 44.6% of volleyball players and 31.9% of basketball players.
Furthermore, prevalence was higher among male athletes (13.5%) than female athletes (5.6%), indicating a 
greater risk in elite male athletes [7]. Tendinopathy is a complex, multifactorial tendon disorder characterized 
by pain, reduced functional capacity, and decreased load tolerance. The most common overuse tendinopathies 
include rotator cuff tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, gluteal tendinopathy, and Achilles tendinopathy [8].
Deviations from normal postural alignment can reduce mechanical efficiency and predispose individuals to 
musculoskeletal and neuromuscular injuries [9]. The lower extremity is the most common site of injury in volley­
ball, accounting for 50–60% of all reported injuries [10, 11]. Poor lower-limb alignment during the deceleration 
phase of closed kinetic chain movements, such as landing, is considered a risk factor for sports-related injuries 
in volleyball players [12].
At the professional and elite levels, the ankle accounts for the greatest proportion of lower-extremity injuries, 
representing 25.9% of all reported injuries [10]. The knee is the second most common site of acute lower-limb 
injuries in volleyball players. Advances in medical imaging have also improved the assessment and character­
ization of sports-related knee injuries, including MRI-based approaches for detailed evaluation of injured knee 
structures [13].
Additionally, the knee is the most frequent site of overuse injuries in the lower extremity among volleyball 
players [2, 10]. PT, a primary source of anterior knee pain, is typically characterized by localized pain at the 
inferior pole of the patella and load-related pain that intensifies during knee extensor activity, particularly during 
movements that require energy storage and release within the patellar tendon [7]. In this regard, Lazaro et al. [14] 
investigated patellar mobility and lower limb kinematics during functional activities in individuals with and with­
out PT. The results indicated that patients with PT exhibited increased lateral patellar mobility compared to those 
without tendinopathy. Additionally, increased hip adduction and greater external ankle rotation were also associ­
ated with PT [14]. Moreover, Khair et al. [15] investigated the modifications in landing mechanics during vertical 
jump tasks in elite volleyball players with PT. The study identified significant alterations in knee joint kinemat­
ics, indicating that PT may influence neuromuscular control and movement patterns during jump landings [15]. 
Therefore, assessing lower-limb alignment during dynamic tasks may be a potential approach for identifying 
individuals at risk for future musculoskeletal pain or injury [16]. In this regard, Shultz et al. [17] examined the 
relationship between lower-extremity alignment characteristics and anterior knee joint laxity. They demonstrated 
that the tibiofemoral angle had the greatest influence on anterior knee laxity [17].
Given the high prevalence of PT among volleyball players likely related to the repetitive jumping and land­
ing demands of the sport and the lack of studies investigating the relationship between PT and frontal-plane 
lower-limb alignment in elite volleyball athletes, the present study aimed to determine whether lower-limb align­
ment differed between affected and unaffected knees in elite male volleyball players with unilateral patellar 
tendinopathy.

https://doi.org/10.1186/s13018-026-07229-w
Materials and methods
This study was reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epide­
miology (STROBE) guidelines for cross-sectional studies [18].
Participants
The present study was a cross-sectional investigation. The source population consisted of elite male volley­
ball players competing in volleyball clubs in Alborz Province, Iran. The study sample included elite male vol­
leyball players, with a mean age of 19.59 ± 2.04 years, a mean height of 191.68 ± 6.72 cm, a mean weight of 
80.59 ± 9.02 kg, and a mean Body Mass Index (BMI) of 22.24 ± 1.88. Initial screening followed the predefined 
inclusion criteria. The inclusion criteria were unilateral PT identified using the Royal London Hospital Test 
(RLHT), male sex, age 18–30 years, and provision of written informed consent. Athletes were excluded if they 
had severe spinal abnormalities identified using the New York test, a history of lower-extremity surgery, or bilat­
eral tendinopathy. Participants were recruited from volleyball clubs in Alborz Province, Iran, between [2025-05-
22] and [2025-08-23], using purposive sampling. Using G*Power for a paired-samples t-test, with an assumed 
effect size of 0.55, α = 0.05, and statistical power of 0.80 (1 − β = 0.80), the required sample size was 22 partici­
pants [19].
Procedures
PT was clinically assessed using the RLHT, which has a reported sensitivity of 88% and specificity of 98% [20]. 
The test was performed with the participant supine and the knee fully extended. The patellar tendon was palpated 
along its entire length, from the proximal to distal attachment at the inferior pole of the patella, to assess for 
localized tenderness. When tenderness was detected, the same area was palpated again, with tenderness absent 
or diminished during knee flexion, indicating PT (Fig. 1) [20]. Both knees were assessed independently using the 
RLHT. Knees demonstrating a positive test were classified as affected, whereas knees with a negative test were 
classified as unaffected.
After identifying participants with PT using the RLHT, they were referred to an Imaging Center in Karaj for 
lower limb radiography. Imaging was conducted using the Payamed system (Iran), with radiation doses adjusted 
appropriately for each region: 80 kV and 200 mA for the pelvis and femur, 65 kV and 125 mA for the knee, and 
55 kV and 100 mA for the tibia and ankle.

Measurement
Radiographic assessment
Radiographic evaluations were conducted using standardized, full-length, bilateral, weight-bearing anterior-pos­
terior X-rays. Participants stood with equal weight distribution on both feet, and their foot position was standard­
ized to ensure reproducibility, particularly regarding foot rotation. The flexion-extension plane was aligned in the 
anterior-posterior direction, and the patella was aligned with the center of the femoral condyles. Typically, the 
feet were rotated externally by 8–10° to achieve proper alignment [21].
Measurement of coronal plane angles
The anatomical and mechanical axes of the femur, tibia, and the entire lower limb were identified, and seven cor­
onal plane angles were subsequently measured. The anatomical axis of the femur was defined along the diaphysis, 
dividing the femoral shaft into two approximately equal halves. In contrast, the tibial anatomical axis was estab­
lished by connecting a point at the proximal tibia to the distal center of the medullary canal. The mechanical axis 
of the femur was determined by connecting the center of the femoral head to the center of the knee joint, often 
identified as the midpoint between the tibial spines. In contrast, the tibial mechanical axis was defined from the 
center of the tibial plateau to the center of the ankle joint [17].
Seven coronal plane angles were measured based on these axes. The anatomical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle 
(aLDFA) was defined as the angle between the anatomical femoral axis and the distal femoral condyles. In con­
trast, the mechanical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (mLDFA) was defined as the angle between the mechanical 
femoral axis and the distal condyles. The anatomical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (aMPTA) represented the 
angle between the anatomical tibial axis and the tibial plateau, and the mechanical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle 
(mMPTA) represented the angle between the mechanical tibial axis and the tibial plateau. The anatomical Tibio­
Femoral Angle (aTFA) was determined as the angle between the anatomical axes of the femur and tibia, and the 
anatomical and mechanical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (aLDTA and mLDTA) were defined as the angles between 
the respective tibial axes and the ankle joint line (Fig. 2) [17].

fected status of the knees. All angles were measured using a standardized procedure.

All participants provided written informed consent prior to the study. Confidentiality of participants’ personal 
information was maintained. Participants were informed that the investigators covered all research-related costs. 
Participants could withdraw from the study at any stage without penalty. The study was conducted in accordance 
with the Declaration of Helsinki. The Ethics Committee of Allameh Tabataba’i University approved the study 
protocol (Ethics Code: IR.ATU.REC.1403.158).

mality using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Paired t-tests were applied to compare the lower limb angles between legs 
with and without PT. All statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 26, with a significance level set

Distal femoral angles (aLDFA, mLDFA) differed by less than one degree, and tibiofemoral angle values varied

Measurement
Radiographic assessment
Radiographic evaluations were conducted using standardized, full-length, bilateral, weight-bearing anterior-pos­
terior X-rays. Participants stood with equal weight distribution on both feet, and their foot position was standard­
ized to ensure reproducibility, particularly regarding foot rotation. The flexion-extension plane was aligned in the 
anterior-posterior direction, and the patella was aligned with the center of the femoral condyles. Typically, the 
feet were rotated externally by 8–10° to achieve proper alignment [21].
Measurement of coronal plane angles
The anatomical and mechanical axes of the femur, tibia, and the entire lower limb were identified, and seven cor­
onal plane angles were subsequently measured. The anatomical axis of the femur was defined along the diaphysis, 
dividing the femoral shaft into two approximately equal halves. In contrast, the tibial anatomical axis was estab­
lished by connecting a point at the proximal tibia to the distal center of the medullary canal. The mechanical axis 
of the femur was determined by connecting the center of the femoral head to the center of the knee joint, often 
identified as the midpoint between the tibial spines. In contrast, the tibial mechanical axis was defined from the 
center of the tibial plateau to the center of the ankle joint [17].
Seven coronal plane angles were measured based on these axes. The anatomical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle 
(aLDFA) was defined as the angle between the anatomical femoral axis and the distal femoral condyles. In con­
trast, the mechanical Lateral Distal Femoral Angle (mLDFA) was defined as the angle between the mechanical 
femoral axis and the distal condyles. The anatomical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle (aMPTA) represented the 
angle between the anatomical tibial axis and the tibial plateau, and the mechanical Medial Proximal Tibial Angle 
(mMPTA) represented the angle between the mechanical tibial axis and the tibial plateau. The anatomical Tibio­
Femoral Angle (aTFA) was determined as the angle between the anatomical axes of the femur and tibia, and the 
anatomical and mechanical Lateral Distal Tibial Angle (aLDTA and mLDTA) were defined as the angles between 
the respective tibial axes and the ankle joint line (Fig. 2) [17].
A single experienced examiner performed radiographic measurements and was blinded to the affected/unaf­
fected status of the knees. All angles were measured using a standardized procedure.
Ethical considerations
All participants provided written informed consent prior to the study. Confidentiality of participants’ personal 
information was maintained. Participants were informed that the investigators covered all research-related costs. 
Participants could withdraw from the study at any stage without penalty. The study was conducted in accordance 
with the Declaration of Helsinki. The Ethics Committee of Allameh Tabataba’i University approved the study 
protocol (Ethics Code: IR.ATU.REC.1403.158).
Statistical analysis
Descriptive statistics (mean ± SD) summarized participants’ age, weight, height, and BMI. We assessed data nor­
mality using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Paired t-tests were applied to compare the lower limb angles between legs 
with and without PT. All statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 26, with a significance level set 
at α = 0.05.

Discussion
The present study examined the relationship between static coronal-plane alignment of the lower limbs and the 
presence of PT in elite volleyball players by comparing affected and unaffected knees within the same individu­
als. Seven radiographic alignment indices were assessed. Statistical analyses revealed no significant differences 
between knees with and without PT. Specifically, p-values ranged from 0.107 to 0.948. Overall, both anatomical 
and mechanical evaluations indicated that static coronal angles were not significantly associated with PT in this 
cohort.
Detailed examination of individual angles revealed minimal variations between affected and unaffected knees. 
Distal femoral angles (aLDFA, mLDFA) differed by less than one degree, and tibiofemoral angle values varied

and distal tibial angles (aLDTA, mLDTA) were comparable between the two conditions. These findings sug­
gest that minor inter-individual variations in distal femoral and proximal tibial geometry, commonly observed

biomechanical evidence indicating that tendon stress is predominantly influenced by dynamic factors, such as 
instantaneous femoral mechanics, transverse rotations, and knee loading during high-intensity functional tasks,

consistent with systematic reviews reporting that static structural factors generally do not substantially influence 
PT development [25]. It also aligns with the general theoretical framework suggesting that PT is predominantly

findings are generalizable. Finally, longitudinal study designs are preferred over cross-sectional approaches, as

Conclusions
The present study found no significant differences in coronal alignment indices, including aMPTA, mMPTA, 
aLDFA, mLDFA, aTFA, aLDTA, and mLDTA, between knees with and without PT in elite volleyball players. 
These findings indicate that static coronal-plane bone alignment is not associated with PT. In contrast, existing 
evidence and biomechanical considerations emphasize that dynamic and modifiable factors such as training load 
and intensity, jumping and landing technique, neuromuscular control, and tendon biological capacity play a more 
prominent role in the onset of this condition. Therefore, clinical and research focus should shift from assessing 
static alignment to managing training load and correcting movement patterns.

This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. The sample was lim­
ited to elite volleyball players, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to female athletes, other 
sports, or athletes with different skill levels. Furthermore, the angular measurements were obtained using static 
radiographic imaging, which does not provide comprehensive information about joint dynamics during sports 
activities. The relatively small sample size may have reduced the statistical power to detect small but potentially 
clinically meaningful differences, thereby increasing the possibility of a Type II error. Therefore, the absence of 
statistically significant differences should be interpreted cautiously and should not be taken as definitive evidence 
that no association exists between coronal-plane alignment and PT. In addition, the analysis was confined to 
coronal plane angles.
In contrast, sagittal and transverse plane angles, which could play a significant role in the development or 
exacerbation of PT, were not assessed. Also, Formal intra- and inter-rater reliability were not assessed, which 
may have introduced measurement error, particularly for small between-knee differences. PT classification was 
based on clinical assessment using the RLHT, without confirmatory ultrasonography or MRI; therefore, some 
uncertainty in PT classification may remain.

appear to play a primary role [27]. These results align with multiple previous studies that did not report strong 
evidence supporting an association between static anatomical or structural alignment and PT. Sprague et al. [26] 
found limited or inconsistent evidence for the association between static anatomical or morphological alignment 
measures and PT, identifying modifiable factors such as greater activity volume, body mass, and countermove­
ment jump height as relevant mediators. Additionally, in an MRI-based study, Crema et al. [28] evaluated knee 
alignment and morphological parameters (including patellofemoral and tibiofemoral alignment) in patients with 
PT versus controls. They found no significant differences in most alignment parameters.
Conversely, some studies have reported associations between alignment or structural/anatomical features and 
tendon pathology, although these relationships were generally weak or context-dependent. Dan et al. [29] reported 
differences in lever arm ratios, patellar tendon angles, and patellar height between symptomatic individuals with 
PT and healthy controls, suggesting that sagittal-plane tendon mechanics may be more relevant than coronal 
tibial alignment. Previous research has also identified several intrinsic risk factors for PT, including quadriceps 
strength, jump performance, flexibility, and tendon loading patterns [26, 30]. However, the role of bony align­
ment, particularly at the tibiofemoral joint, remains unclear. Although abnormal lower limb alignment has been 
proposed as a factor influencing patellar tracking and patellofemoral joint stress [22], static coronal bone align­
ment cannot be considered a primary or independent determinant of PT in athletic populations [30].
From a biomechanical perspective, several factors may explain the absence of observed differences. First, 
angular values in athletes typically fall within a narrow physiological range, so minor inter-individual varia­
tions are unlikely to meaningfully alter tendon loading patterns. Additionally, the musculoskeletal system has 
substantial compensatory capacity, with small deviations at one joint often offset by adjustments at adjacent 
joints and changes in muscle activation, effectively neutralizing the potential impact of tibial or femoral angles 
[31]. Second, the patellar tendon loads most during high-intensity dynamic tasks, such as jumping, landing, and 
change-of-direction movements. Laboratory and modeling studies show that variables such as knee flexion angle 
at landing, torque generation rate, and quadriceps-hamstring activation patterns most strongly influence tendon 
strain and stress.
In contrast, static coronal measures have limited ability to explain these dynamic forces [26, 27]. Therefore, it 
can be concluded that proximal tibial alignment in the coronal plane, as a static variable, is not associated with 
PT in athletes. Accordingly, the combination of the present numerical data and theoretical evidence suggests that 
clinical and research focus for predicting and preventing PT should be directed toward dynamic and modifiable 
factors, such as training load management[27], enhancement of jump-landing mechanics [32], targeted strength 
training [33], and imaging-based monitoring of tendon structural adaptations [34], as these factors have demon­
strated the strongest associations with the incidence and progression of PT.
Finally, the multifactorial nature of tendinopathy, encompassing training load, tendon capacity, biological 
responses, and environmental factors, precludes any single static coronal variable from being decisive [25, 35, 
36]. This explains why some athletes with apparently normal alignment can develop tendinopathy, while others 
with structural deviations remain asymptomatic[37]. Based on the findings of the present study, Future research 
should focus on sagittal and transverse plane alignment, as patellar tendon loading is predominantly influenced 
by these planes. The use of dynamic imaging techniques, such as functional MRI, is recommended to capture in 
vivo tendon and joint behavior during sport-specific activities. A multifactorial approach that integrates biologi­
cal factors, such as tissue healing capacity and genetic predisposition, with mechanical variables could provide 
a more comprehensive understanding of PT etiology. The statistical analyses did not account for key potential 
confounders, such as previous history of lower-limb injury, weekly training load and intensity, limb dominance, 
and foot arch status. These factors may influence both lower-limb alignment and the development of patellar 
tendinopathy and therefore could not be incorporated as covariates in the present analyses. Future studies should 
assess and include these variables as covariates. The sample consists exclusively of elite male volleyball players 
from Alborz Province, with a narrow age range. This significantly restricts the generalizability of the findings to 
female athletes, nonelite or amateur players, or athletes from other sports. Further studies involving female ath­
letes, different competitive levels, sports, and geographic populations are warranted to determine whether these

findings are generalizable. Finally, longitudinal study designs are preferred over cross-sectional approaches, as 
they allow for clearer assessment of the temporal effects of various risk factors on tendon health.
Conclusions
The present study found no significant differences in coronal alignment indices, including aMPTA, mMPTA, 
aLDFA, mLDFA, aTFA, aLDTA, and mLDTA, between knees with and without PT in elite volleyball players. 
These findings indicate that static coronal-plane bone alignment is not associated with PT. In contrast, existing 
evidence and biomechanical considerations emphasize that dynamic and modifiable factors such as training load 
and intensity, jumping and landing technique, neuromuscular control, and tendon biological capacity play a more 
prominent role in the onset of this condition. Therefore, clinical and research focus should shift from assessing 
static alignment to managing training load and correcting movement patterns.
Limitations of the study
This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. The sample was lim­
ited to elite volleyball players, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to female athletes, other 
sports, or athletes with different skill levels. Furthermore, the angular measurements were obtained using static 
radiographic imaging, which does not provide comprehensive information about joint dynamics during sports 
activities. The relatively small sample size may have reduced the statistical power to detect small but potentially 
clinically meaningful differences, thereby increasing the possibility of a Type II error. Therefore, the absence of 
statistically significant differences should be interpreted cautiously and should not be taken as definitive evidence 
that no association exists between coronal-plane alignment and PT. In addition, the analysis was confined to 
coronal plane angles.
In contrast, sagittal and transverse plane angles, which could play a significant role in the development or 
exacerbation of PT, were not assessed. Also, Formal intra- and inter-rater reliability were not assessed, which 
may have introduced measurement error, particularly for small between-knee differences. PT classification was 
based on clinical assessment using the RLHT, without confirmatory ultrasonography or MRI; therefore, some 
uncertainty in PT classification may remain.
