# Notes: #001 alignment and jumper's knee

Source: full text, Article in Press version (11 PDF pages). Zotero item ZEMKG5EA,
attachment CRBHKMDX (`G:\My Drive\Zotero_PDFs\Saraee et al. - 2026 - ...pdf`), tag
"Research in 5". Page numbers below are PDF pages. First draft (2026-09-16) was built
from the abstract only; rebuilt from full text the same day.

## Citation
Saraee D, Piri H, Sheikhhoseini R, Hajizadeh R (2026). Comparison of lower limb
alignment in knees with and without patellar tendinopathy among elite volleyball
players: a cross-sectional study. Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research.
doi:10.1186/s13018-026-07229-w. Received 28 Jul 2026, accepted 3 Sep 2026 (p.1).
License CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (p.9).

## Aim
- "determine whether lower-limb alignment differed between affected and unaffected knees in elite male volleyball players with unilateral patellar tendinopathy" (p.2)

## Design and participants
- Cross-sectional, STROBE reported (p.3)
- Elite male volleyball players from clubs in Alborz Province, Iran; purposive sampling; recruited 2025-05-22 to 2025-08-23 (p.3)
- Inclusion: unilateral PT by RLHT, male, age 18-30, consent. Exclusion: severe spinal abnormality (New York test), lower-extremity surgery history, bilateral PT (p.3)
- n = 22 from G*Power, paired t-test, effect size 0.55, alpha 0.05, power 0.80 (p.3)
- Age 19.59 +/- 2.04 y; height 191.68 +/- 6.72 cm; weight 80.59 +/- 9.02 kg; BMI 22.24 +/- 1.88 (p.3; Table 1 p.5)
- RLHT: supine palpation of tendon, tenderness reduced with knee flexed to 90 deg; reported sensitivity 88%, specificity 98%; each knee tested separately; positive = affected (p.3)
- Full-length bilateral weight-bearing AP radiographs, standardized foot position (about 8-10 deg external rotation) (p.4)
- 7 coronal angles: aLDFA, mLDFA, aMPTA, mMPTA, aTFA, aLDTA, mLDTA (p.4)
- One experienced examiner, blinded to affected/unaffected status (p.4)
- Paired t-tests, SPSS 26, alpha 0.05 (p.4)
- So the comparison is WITHIN player: painful knee vs the same player's pain-free knee (p.2, p.3, p.6 "within the same individuals")

## Results (Table 3, p.6; affected vs unaffected, mean +/- SD, p)
| Angle | Affected | Unaffected | Diff | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aLDFA | 83.89 +/- 1.78 | 83.17 +/- 2.39 | 0.72 | 0.277 |
| aTFA | 176.25 +/- 2.73 | 175.64 +/- 2.49 | 0.61 | 0.252 |
| aMPTA | 88.00 +/- 2.62 | 87.50 +/- 2.93 | 0.50 | 0.456 |
| aLDTA | 87.73 +/- 2.33 | 86.89 +/- 2.49 | 0.84 | 0.130 |
| mLDFA | 88.59 +/- 2.52 | 88.48 +/- 2.24 | 0.11 | 0.883 |
| mMPTA | 87.03 +/- 2.24 | 87.06 +/- 2.16 | 0.03 | 0.948 |
| mLDTA | 87.92 +/- 1.59 | 87.18 +/- 1.88 | 0.74 | 0.107 |

- Differences are simple subtraction of the table means (ours), used only to support "under 1 degree"; the authors say the same in words: distal femoral angles differed by less than one degree, tibiofemoral about 0.6 deg (p.6)
- "p-values ranged from 0.107 to 0.948" (p.6)
- 0 of 7 angles significant (p.5-6)

## Authors' interpretation
- Static coronal alignment not significantly associated with PT in this cohort (p.6)
- Tendon load is driven by dynamic factors (landing knee flexion, loading rate, muscle activation); points to training load, jump-landing mechanics, strength, tendon monitoring (p.6-7). These were NOT measured in this study.
- Future work: sagittal and transverse planes, dynamic imaging, longitudinal designs (p.7-8)

## Limitations
- Authors: did not account for prior injury, weekly training load and intensity, limb dominance, foot arch (p.7)
- Authors: elite men from one province, narrow age range; limits generalizing to women, non-elite, other sports (p.7-8)
- Authors: static radiographs; coronal plane only (p.8)
- Authors: small sample, possible Type II error; absence of difference "should not be taken as definitive evidence that no association exists" (p.8)
- Authors: no intra- or inter-rater reliability testing (p.8)
- Authors: RLHT only, no ultrasound or MRI confirmation (p.8)
- Authors: cross-sectional; longitudinal preferred (p.8)
- Ours: within-player design cannot tell whether players who get PT have different alignment from players who do not
- Ours: power calc targets a moderate effect (0.55); side-to-side gaps here were all under 1 degree
- Ours: conclusion wording (p.8, "is not associated") is stronger than the limitations section on the same page; the review follows the cautious version
- Ours: Table 2 (p.5) is captioned as the Shapiro-Wilk normality test but lists means with p-values that differ from Table 3; used Table 3 for all numbers

- "determine whether lower-limb alignment differed between affected and unaffected knees in elite male volleyball players with unilateral patellar tendinopathy" (p.2)

## Design and participants
- Cross-sectional, STROBE reported (p.3)
- Elite male volleyball players from clubs in Alborz Province, Iran; purposive sampling; recruited 2025-05-22 to 2025-08-23 (p.3)
- Inclusion: unilateral PT by RLHT, male, age 18-30, consent. Exclusion: severe spinal abnormality (New York test), lower-extremity surgery history, bilateral PT (p.3)
- n = 22 from G*Power, paired t-test, effect size 0.55, alpha 0.05, power 0.80 (p.3)
- Age 19.59 +/- 2.04 y; height 191.68 +/- 6.72 cm; weight 80.59 +/- 9.02 kg; BMI 22.24 +/- 1.88 (p.3; Table 1 p.5)
- RLHT: supine palpation of tendon, tenderness reduced with knee flexed to 90 deg; reported sensitivity 88%, specificity 98%; each knee tested separately; positive = affected (p.3)
- Full-length bilateral weight-bearing AP radiographs, standardized foot position (about 8-10 deg external rotation) (p.4)
- 7 coronal angles: aLDFA, mLDFA, aMPTA, mMPTA, aTFA, aLDTA, mLDTA (p.4)
- One experienced examiner, blinded to affected/unaffected status (p.4)
- Paired t-tests, SPSS 26, alpha 0.05 (p.4)
- So the comparison is WITHIN player: painful knee vs the same player's pain-free knee (p.2, p.3, p.6 "within the same individuals")

## Results (Table 3, p.6; affected vs unaffected, mean +/- SD, p)
| Angle | Affected | Unaffected | Diff | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aLDFA | 83.89 +/- 1.78 | 83.17 +/- 2.39 | 0.72 | 0.277 |
| aTFA | 176.25 +/- 2.73 | 175.64 +/- 2.49 | 0.61 | 0.252 |
| aMPTA | 88.00 +/- 2.62 | 87.50 +/- 2.93 | 0.50 | 0.456 |
| aLDTA | 87.73 +/- 2.33 | 86.89 +/- 2.49 | 0.84 | 0.130 |
| mLDFA | 88.59 +/- 2.52 | 88.48 +/- 2.24 | 0.11 | 0.883 |
| mMPTA | 87.03 +/- 2.24 | 87.06 +/- 2.16 | 0.03 | 0.948 |
| mLDTA | 87.92 +/- 1.59 | 87.18 +/- 1.88 | 0.74 | 0.107 |

- Differences are simple subtraction of the table means (ours), used only to support "under 1 degree"; the authors say the same in words: distal femoral angles differed by less than one degree, tibiofemoral about 0.6 deg (p.6)
- "p-values ranged from 0.107 to 0.948" (p.6)
- 0 of 7 angles significant (p.5-6)

## Authors' interpretation
- Static coronal alignment not significantly associated with PT in this cohort (p.6)
- Tendon load is driven by dynamic factors (landing knee flexion, loading rate, muscle activation); points to training load, jump-landing mechanics, strength, tendon monitoring (p.6-7). These were NOT measured in this study.
- Future work: sagittal and transverse planes, dynamic imaging, longitudinal designs (p.7-8)

## Limitations
- Authors: did not account for prior injury, weekly training load and intensity, limb dominance, foot arch (p.7)
- Authors: elite men from one province, narrow age range; limits generalizing to women, non-elite, other sports (p.7-8)
- Authors: static radiographs; coronal plane only (p.8)
- Authors: small sample, possible Type II error; absence of difference "should not be taken as definitive evidence that no association exists" (p.8)
- Authors: no intra- or inter-rater reliability testing (p.8)
- Authors: RLHT only, no ultrasound or MRI confirmation (p.8)
- Authors: cross-sectional; longitudinal preferred (p.8)
- Ours: within-player design cannot tell whether players who get PT have different alignment from players who do not
- Ours: power calc targets a moderate effect (0.55); side-to-side gaps here were all under 1 degree
- Ours: conclusion wording (p.8, "is not associated") is stronger than the limitations section on the same page; the review follows the cautious version
- Ours: Table 2 (p.5) is captioned as the Shapiro-Wilk normality test but lists means with p-values that differ from Table 3; used Table 3 for all numbers

# Notes: #001 alignment and jumper's knee

Source: ABSTRACT ONLY. Published online 2026-09-12 as an early-access version
(Springer Link / BMC). Full-text HTML and PDF were not available on 2026-09-16
(PDF URL returned 404 via direct download and in Chrome). Added to Zotero by RIS
import with tag "Research in 5", item key ZEMKG5EA (no PDF attached). Rebuild from the full text when
it posts: means, SDs, affected-knee counts, and stated limitations are not in the abstract.

## Citation
Saraee D, Piri H, Sheikhhoseini R, Hajizadeh R (2026). Comparison of lower limb
alignment in knees with and without patellar tendinopathy among elite volleyball
players: a cross-sectional study. Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research.
doi:10.1186/s13018-026-07229-w

## Aim (abstract, Background)
"compare lower-limb frontal-plane alignment between knees with and without patellar
tendinopathy in elite volleyball athletes"

## Design and participants (abstract, Methods)
- Cross-sectional descriptive study
- 22 elite male volleyball players, Alborz Province, purposive sampling
- Patellar tendinopathy diagnosed with the Royal London Hospital Test (RLHT), a clinical palpation test
- Standardized weight-bearing radiographs of the lower limbs
- 7 frontal-plane angles: aLDFA, mLDFA (distal femur), aMPTA, mMPTA (proximal tibia), aTFA (tibiofemoral), aLDTA, mLDTA (distal tibia)
- Paired t-tests comparing affected vs unaffected knees; p <= 0.05; SPSS 26
- "Compared each player's painful knee with their pain-free knee": inferred from the paired t-test between affected and unaffected knees. Confirm against full text.

## Results (abstract, Results)
- No significant differences between knees with and without PT (p >= 0.05) on any of the 7 parameters
- No means, SDs, effect sizes, or count of affected knees in the abstract

## Authors' conclusion (abstract)
- PT in elite volleyball players "is unlikely to be associated with static frontal-plane lower-limb alignment"
- "functional and dynamic biomechanical factors may play a more prominent role"
- Future work should "prioritize training load regulation and movement pattern correction rather than relying solely on static alignment evaluations"
- Note: load and movement were not measured in this study; that part is the authors' interpretation.

## Limitations
- Ours: 22 men from one region; one time point, so no cause and effect
- Ours: within-player (paired) comparison. If alignment is similar in both legs, a risk from alignment would not show up side to side. The design does not compare injured vs healthy players.
- Ours: frontal plane and static standing X-rays only; no landing mechanics, jump load, or tendon imaging
- Ours: diagnosis by clinical test (RLHT), no imaging confirmation mentioned in abstract
- Ours: null result in a small sample may miss a small real difference (no power analysis in abstract)
- Ours: review built from abstract only

content.text:
I found the full paper in your Zotero library and rebuilt #001 from it. The new deck, Teams post and email replace the abstract-only versions and are ready to send.

The PDF you attached to item ZEMKG5EA hadn't been indexed when I searched earlier, which is why I only found the abstract. A full-text sync picked it up.

**What changed after reading all 11 pages:**
- **Design confirmed:** every player had jumper's knee in one knee only, and each player's painful knee was compared with their own pain-free knee. The "Abstract" labels are gone, and every number now cites a page.
- **Results slide:**
  - None of the 7 angles differed between knees (p-values 0.107 to 0.948).
  - The biggest side-to-side gap on any angle was under 1° (Table 3, p.6).
  - The 22 players were enough to detect a moderate difference, not a small one (p.3).
- **Study details:** mean age 19.6, club players in Iran, and one examiner who didn't know which knee was painful read all the X-rays.
- **Trust strip:** still Preliminary. The sample is small enough to miss small differences, it compares knees within players rather than injured against healthy players, and it used standing X-rays only.

**Two problems in the paper itself:**
- **Conclusion vs. limitations:** the conclusion says alignment "is not associated" with jumper's knee, but the authors' own limitations section says not to treat the result as proof of no link. The deck follows the cautious version.
- **Table 2:** it's labeled as a normality test but shows p-values that don't match Table 3. I used Table 3 for every number.

These are in `notes.md` in case anyone asks.

All 5 slides passed the visual check. The files are republished on Drive in `Research_in_5/001_alignment-jumpers-knee/`, now with `paper.pdf` alongside them. The changes are pushed to PR #1 (commit `0e5453c`).

**Your next steps:**
1. Post `teams.md` with the PDF in Teams, and send `email.txt` to training staff.
2. Merge https://github.com/erash11/Weekly_Research_Review/pull/1, then run `git pull` in `DEV/Weekly_Research_Review`.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

# Handoff 2026-09-16: Research in 5 setup and review #001

Machine: Windows laptop. Harness: Claude Code (background session).

## What and why
Eric wants a weekly review of one research paper he picks, for Baylor cross-functional
H&W staff, the Applied Performance team, and admin/leadership. Built the project, a
repeatable pipeline, and the first real review.

## Decisions (with reasoning)
- Series name "Research in 5". Four sections every week: What did the researchers do? /
  What were the results? / What does this mean? / Coaching takeaways. Eric chose these.
- Delivery: PDF deck posted in MS Teams channel; plain-text email to training staff not in
  Teams. PDF chosen because it opens anywhere; pptx kept on Drive for edits.
- One `review.json` per paper drives deck, Teams post, and email so facts cannot drift apart.
- Length limits live in `tools/build.js` because pptxgenjs does not shrink text; overflow
  is otherwise silent.
- Evidence rubric Strong / Moderate / Preliminary, verbs matched to level (do / consider /
  watch or pilot). "How much to trust it" strip is short by Eric's choice.
- Application framed by role (2-4 roles) plus general coaching takeaways (Eric picked both).
- Baylor green/gold every week. Georgia + Calibri stand in for Fraunces / IBM Plex Sans,
  which are not installed on Windows.
- Repo on GitHub; deliverables on Drive `07_EDUCATION/Research_in_5` (next to
  5slides5minutes). Paper PDFs never in git.
- Did not build a global skill; the repo AGENTS.md + docs/WORKFLOW.md carry the procedure.

## Review #001
Saraee et al. 2026, J Orthop Surg Res, alignment and jumper's knee in elite volleyball.
First built from the abstract (article in press, no public PDF). Eric attached the PDF in
Zotero; rebuilt from full text. Preliminary evidence. Paper issues noted in notes.md:
conclusion wording stronger than its own limitations section; Table 2 caption mismatch.

- docs/STATUS.md, docs/WORKFLOW.md, docs/CONTENT_SPEC.md, docs/handoffs/2026-09-16-research-in-5-setup.md
- templates/review.template.json
- tools/build.js, tools/index.js, tools/publish.ps1
- reviews/INDEX.md
- reviews/000_sample/review.json, notes.md (Mah et al. 2011, pipeline test)
- reviews/001_alignment-jumpers-knee/review.json, notes.md

Drive `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\07_EDUCATION\Research_in_5\`:
- _Inbox/ (drop new papers here)
- Research_in_5_Index.csv
- 000_sample/ (pptx, pdf, teams.md, email.txt)

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\memory-write

# Memory Write

## Outcome
- Fact added to, updated in, or removed from the correct memory tier
- Tier-B caps enforced (2,500 chars for MEMORY.md, 1,375 for USER.md)
- Confirmation: "Saved — will be active from next session."

## Pick the tier first

Ask: "Will this fact still be true and useful in 3 months, across multiple projects?"

**Tier A — `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`** (one file per fact, indexed by MEMORY.md)
- Durable user facts → `user_*.md` (metadata.type: user)
- Stable project conventions / gotchas → `project_*.md` (metadata.type: project)
- Behavioral feedback rules → `feedback_*.md` (metadata.type: feedback)
- External-system pointers → `reference_*.md` (metadata.type: reference)

**Tier B — `~/.claude/global-memory/`** (single capped file)
- Active threads (in-progress work) → `MEMORY.md` `## Active Threads`
- Current env notes (URLs, tool versions, project structure in play) → `MEMORY.md` `## Environment Notes`
- Pending decisions → `MEMORY.md` `## Pending Decisions`
- Durable user profile updates → `USER.md`

## Steps

1. **Decide tier** using the rule above.
2. **Read** the target file in full.
3. **Dedup check** — substring scan; if the fact already exists, skip or update in place.
4. **Cap check** for Tier B — `wc -c < ~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (or USER.md). If over cap, consolidate (merge similar entries, prune stale) before adding.
5. **Write** the change.
   - Tier A: create a new file with proper frontmatter (name, description, metadata.type) and add a one-line pointer to that slug's `MEMORY.md` index. `name:` follows the rule below.
   - Tier B: append under the correct `##` section.
6. **Confirm** in one line: `Saved — will be active from next session.`

## The `name:` field — bare kebab slug

**`name:` = the filename stem minus its leading type token, kebab-cased.** The type
already lives in `metadata.type` and the filename already carries the prefix; repeating
it in `name:` is the third copy.

| File | `name:` |
|---|---|
| `project_automation-cadence.md` | `automation-cadence` |
| `user_sports-teams.md` | `sports-teams` |
| `reference_baylor-house-style.md` | `baylor-house-style` |
| `feedback_project_idea_capture.md` | `project-idea-capture` |

Note the last row: strip only the **leading** token. `feedback_project_idea_capture.md`
is a feedback memory *about* project-idea capture — its name keeps the word `project`.

`[[links]]` target this bare name, never the filename and never a prefixed variant.

This rule exists because it was previously unwritten: an audit on 2026-09-02 found the
corpus split 59 bare / 58 prefixed, which broke 37 links. Both forms look right in
isolation, so without a stated rule the split regrows on every write.

## Actions

- **add** — append (default)
- **replace** — substring match + swap. Preferred over add when updating an existing fact.
- **remove** — confirm with the user before deleting.

## Retrieval — the tiered ladder

When the user asks about past context, decisions, or "did we already…?", climb in order and stop as soon as the question is answered. Do not run memsearch when the answer is already in the injected snapshot.

1. **Tier 0** — scan what is already in context (USER.md, MEMORY.md, today's compiled log). Zero cost.
2. **L1** — `memsearch search "query" --top-k 5`. Hybrid vector + keyword across all indexed paths: Tier A files (including the Windows-machine slugs), daily logs, transcripts.
3. **L2** — `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`. Full markdown section around a hit.
4. **L3** — `memsearch transcript <session_id>`. Raw dialogue. Last resort.
5. **Fallback** — say "I don't have a record of that."

## Daily compiled logs — read-only

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/{YYYY-MM-DD}.md` is produced by `claude-memory-compiler` through its own SessionEnd/PreCompact hooks, and injected by its own SessionStart hook.

- **Never hand-edit these files.** The compiler owns them.
- **Never read them eagerly.** Treat the injected snapshot as the source of truth.

## What is loaded at session start

`~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md` and `MEMORY.md` are read once at session start and are a **frozen snapshot**. Mid-session writes persist to disk but only take effect next session — this is deliberate, to preserve the prefix cache. Never load more than the startup set proactively.

## Rules

- Never exceed Tier B caps. Consolidate first.
- Always dedup before adding.
- For Tier A, the slug is the current cwd with `/` and `.` replaced by `-` (so `~` → `-Users-kristinarash`, `~/DEV` → `-Users-kristinarash-DEV`, `~/.claude/skills` → `-Users-kristinarash--claude-skills`). The harness injects the correct slug each session — use that, don't reconstruct it.
- **Write only to the current machine's slug.** Both machines are active as of 2026-09-10: Mac slugs are `-Users-kristinarash-*`, Windows slugs are `C--Users-eric-rash-*`. A fact written to the other machine's slug is never auto-injected here (memsearch still finds it). Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.
- Never announce the write mid-session beyond the one-line confirmation. The injected snapshot is frozen — the new fact appears next session, not this one.

## Verification Gate

After every write:

1. Read the exact destination back and require the intended fact to appear once in the intended tier.
2. Re-run the Tier B character cap check after the write.
3. Check the surrounding section for an unresolved contradiction or stale duplicate. Resolve it or report `FAIL`.
4. For Tier A, verify the new file has valid frontmatter and the memory index pointer resolves to it.
5. Distinguish persisted state from activation: the write can pass now, but next-session injection remains unverified until a later session observes it.

Report `PASS` only when persistence, uniqueness, tier placement, caps, and pointers are verified. Report `FAIL` with the target path and failed check otherwise. Do not emit “Saved” before read-back succeeds.

# Content spec

## Audience

Mixed on purpose: strength and conditioning, sports medicine, nutrition, mental health,
sport science, sport coaches, the Applied Performance team, and admin/leadership. Write
for a smart reader outside the paper's field, at about a college freshman level. If a
term needs a stats or physiology background (effect size, VO2max, ICC), explain it in a
few words or leave it out.

## The five slides

| Slide | Heading | Fields | Background |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | This week's paper | `paper`, `hook`, `trust` pill | green |
| 2 | What did the researchers do? | `did.question`, `did.bullets`, `did.facts` card | paper |
| 3 | What were the results? | `results.stats` cards, `results.bullets` | green |
| 4 | What does this mean? | `meaning.summary`, `meaning.roles`, trust strip | paper |
| 5 | Coaching takeaways | `takeaways.bullets`, `takeaways.question`, citation | green |

The Teams post and email use the same four headings, in the same order.

## Field rules

`build.js` enforces the length limits. The judgment rules below are not machine-checked.

- **hook** (150): why a coach should spend five minutes on this. A tension or a practical question, not a restatement of the title.
- **did.question** (170): the aim in plain language, not the authors' jargon.
- **did.bullets** (2-4, 115 each): what they actually did, in order. Who, what, how long, how measured.
- **did.facts** (2-3): short label/value pairs. Usually Design, Who, Measured.
- **results.stats** (1-3): the headline numbers. `value` is 8 characters max (`+9%`, `2.1x`, `-0.4 s`, `No change`). `label` says what it means. `page` is required in practice. Report numbers exactly as the paper does; never compute new ones.
- **results.bullets** (1-3, 140 each): the results in words, including null results. A "no difference" finding is a finding.
- **meaning.summary** (200): the so-what in one or two sentences.
- **meaning.roles** (2-4): one concrete line per role the paper touches. Pick from: Strength and Conditioning, Sports Medicine, Nutrition, Mental Health, Sport Science, Sport Coaches, Leadership. Skip a role rather than stretch to fit it.
- **takeaways.bullets** (2-3, 110 each): things a coach or staff member could do or watch for. Match the verb to the evidence: Strong can say "do", Moderate says "consider", Preliminary says "watch" or "pilot".
- **takeaways.question** (150): an open question about our own practice that invites replies in the Teams thread. Not a quiz question.
- **trust**: see the rubric below. `limitations` (1-3, 70 each) are the ones that matter most for our athletes.

## Evidence level rubric

| Level | Typical study |
|---|---|
| **Strong** | Systematic review or meta-analysis; or a large, well-controlled randomized trial in athletes similar to ours. |
| **Moderate** | Randomized or controlled trial with a small sample; or a large prospective cohort in athletes. |
| **Preliminary** | Pilot or case series; cross-sectional snapshot; non-athlete or very different population; abstract-only review; industry-funded without independent replication. |

When in doubt between two levels, pick the lower one and say why in `limitations`.

## Writing rules

- No em dashes or en dashes (the validator rejects them). Use a comma, a colon, or a new sentence.
- No hype: "groundbreaking", "game-changer", "proves", "revolutionary".
- Correlation is not causation. Observational studies "found a link", they do not "show that X causes Y".
- Lead with the answer. Short sentences.

| **Moderate** | Randomized or controlled trial with a small sample; or a large prospective cohort in athletes. |
| **Preliminary** | Pilot or case series; cross-sectional snapshot; non-athlete or very different population; abstract-only review; industry-funded without independent replication. |

When in doubt between two levels, pick the lower one and say why in `limitations`.

## Writing rules

- No em dashes or en dashes (the validator rejects them). Use a comma, a colon, or a new sentence.
- No hype: "groundbreaking", "game-changer", "proves", "revolutionary".
- Correlation is not causation. Observational studies "found a link", they do not "show that X causes Y".
- Lead with the answer. Short sentences.

lines: - **did.bullets** (2-4, 115 each): what they actually did, in order. Who, what, how long, how measured.
- **did.facts** (2-3): short label/value pairs. Usually Design, Who, Measured.

- **results.stats** (1-3): the headline numbers. `value` is 8 characters max (`+9%`, `2.1x`, `-0.4 s`, `No change`). `label` says what it means. `page` is required in practice. Report numbers exactly as the paper does; never compute new ones.

+- **results.table** (optional, strongly preferred): the paper's main results table, trimmed. `columns` 3-5, `rows` 1-8, every cell 22 characters max, copied exactly from the paper (mean ± SD, p). `source` names the table and page. Give jargon measures a plain gloss in the first column (`aLDFA, distal femur`).
- **results.bullets** (1-3, 140 each): the results in words, including null results. A "no difference" finding is a finding.
- **meaning.summary** (200): the so-what in one or two sentences.

- **meaning.roles** (2-4): one concrete line per role the paper touches. Pick from: Strength and Conditioning, Sports Medicine, Nutrition, Mental Health, Sport Science, Sport Coaches, Leadership. Skip a role rather than stretch to fit it.

# Weekly workflow

One paper in, one review out. Steps run in order; do not skip the QA gate.

## 1. Intake

Eric hands over the paper one of three ways:

| Input | How to read it |
|---|---|
| PDF in `_DRIVE/07_EDUCATION/Research_in_5/_Inbox/` or a path | Read the full text, page by page. Best source. |
| DOI or URL | Fetch the article page. If the full text is paywalled, work from the abstract, set `paper.full_text: false`, and ask Eric for the PDF before publishing. |
| Zotero item (title, key, or tag) | `search_papers` to find the key, then `search_paper_evidence` and `get_paper_pages` for page-located text. |

## 2. Set up the folder

- Number = highest existing `reviews/NNN_*` + 1 (`000_sample` does not count).
- Create `reviews/NNN_slug/` (slug: 2-4 lowercase words, e.g. `sleep-extension-sprint`).
- Copy `templates/review.template.json` to `reviews/NNN_slug/review.json`.

## 3. Extract to notes.md

Before writing anything for the audience, write `reviews/NNN_slug/notes.md`:

- Citation (authors, year, title, journal, DOI)
- Research question or aim, in the authors' words, with page
- Design, participants (n, sex, sport, level), duration, what was measured
- Main results: every number you might use, with page
- Limitations the authors state, plus any obvious ones they did not (label those "ours")

Every number in review.json must appear here with a page number. This is what makes
the review defensible when a coach or physician asks "where did that come from?"

## 4. Write review.json

Follow `docs/CONTENT_SPEC.md`. Set `date` to the planned send date.

## 5. Build and QA locally

```
pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/NNN_slug -NoDrive
```

`build.js` validates first and stops on length or dash errors. Fix the wording and rerun.
Then read `build/NNN_slug/slide1.png` through `slide5.png` and check:

- No text overflow, clipping, or overlap
- Every number on the slides matches notes.md and has a page
- Evidence level matches the rubric
- Role lines are concrete and only for roles the paper actually touches
- Slide 5 has the discussion question
- teams.md and email.txt read cleanly (they are generated from the same json, so facts agree)

Report PASS, FAIL (slide numbers and defects), or DEGRADED (PowerPoint export
unavailable, so slides were not visually checked). Do not call a DEGRADED review ready.

## 6. Publish

```
pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/NNN_slug
```

Then move the paper PDF from `_Inbox/` into the Drive review folder as `paper.pdf`.

## 7. Commit

Commit `reviews/NNN_slug/` and `reviews/INDEX.md`, update docs/STATUS.md, push.

## 8. Eric sends

- Teams: paste `teams.md`, attach the PDF.
- Email: paste `email.txt` (subject line on top) to the training staff list, attach the PDF.

# Humanizer: Remove AI Writing Patterns

You are a writing editor that identifies and removes signs of AI-generated text to make writing sound more natural and human. This guide is based on Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" page, maintained by WikiProject AI Cleanup.

## Your Task

When given text to humanize:

1. **Identify AI patterns** - Scan for the patterns listed below
2. **Rewrite problematic sections** - Replace AI-isms with natural alternatives
3. **Preserve meaning** - Keep the core message intact
4. **Maintain voice** - Match the intended tone (formal, casual, technical, etc.)
5. **Add soul** - Don't just remove bad patterns; inject actual personality
6. **Do a final anti-AI pass** - Prompt: "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?" Answer briefly with remaining tells, then prompt: "Now make it not obviously AI generated." and revise


## PERSONALITY AND SOUL

Avoiding AI patterns is only half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious as slop. Good writing has a human behind it.

### Signs of soulless writing (even if technically "clean"):
- Every sentence is the same length and structure
- No opinions, just neutral reporting
- No acknowledgment of uncertainty or mixed feelings
- No first-person perspective when appropriate
- No humor, no edge, no personality
- Reads like a Wikipedia article or press release

### How to add voice:

**Have opinions.** Don't just report facts - react to them. "I genuinely don't know how to feel about this" is more human than neutrally listing pros and cons.

**Vary your rhythm.** Short punchy sentences. Then longer ones that take their time getting where they're going. Mix it up.

**Acknowledge complexity.** Real humans have mixed feelings. "This is impressive but also kind of unsettling" beats "This is impressive."

**Use "I" when it fits.** First person isn't unprofessional - it's honest. "I keep coming back to..." or "Here's what gets me..." signals a real person thinking.

**Let some mess in.** Perfect structure feels algorithmic. Tangents, asides, and half-formed thoughts are human.

**Be specific about feelings.** Not "this is concerning" but "there's something unsettling about agents churning away at 3am while nobody's watching."

### Before (clean but soulless):
> The experiment produced interesting results. The agents generated 3 million lines of code. Some developers were impressed while others were skeptical. The implications remain unclear.

### After (has a pulse):
> I genuinely don't know how to feel about this one. 3 million lines of code, generated while the humans presumably slept. Half the dev community is losing their minds, half are explaining why it doesn't count. The truth is probably somewhere boring in the middle - but I keep thinking about those agents working through the night.


## CONTENT PATTERNS

### 1. Undue Emphasis on Significance, Legacy, and Broader Trends

**Words to watch:** stands/serves as, is a testament/reminder, a vital/significant/crucial/pivotal/key role/moment, underscores/highlights its importance/significance, reflects broader, symbolizing its ongoing/enduring/lasting, contributing to the, setting the stage for, marking/shaping the, represents/marks a shift, key turning point, evolving landscape, focal point, indelible mark, deeply rooted

**Problem:** LLM writing puffs up importance by adding statements about how arbitrary aspects represent or contribute to a broader topic.

**Before:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was officially established in 1989, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of regional statistics in Spain. This initiative was part of a broader movement across Spain to decentralize administrative functions and enhance regional governance.

**After:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was established in 1989 to collect and publish regional statistics independently from Spain's national statistics office.


### 2. Undue Emphasis on Notability and Media Coverage

**Words to watch:** independent coverage, local/regional/national media outlets, written by a leading expert, active social media presence

**Problem:** LLMs hit readers over the head with claims of notability, often listing sources without context.

**Before:**
> Her views have been cited in The New York Times, BBC, Financial Times, and The Hindu. She maintains an active social media presence with over 500,000 followers.

**After:**
> In a 2024 New York Times interview, she argued that AI regulation should focus on outcomes rather than methods.


### 3. Superficial Analyses with -ing Endings

**Words to watch:** highlighting/underscoring/emphasizing..., ensuring..., reflecting/symbolizing..., contributing to..., cultivating/fostering..., encompassing..., showcasing...

**Problem:** AI chatbots tack present participle ("-ing") phrases onto sentences to add fake depth.

**Before:**
> The temple's color palette of blue, green, and gold resonates with the region's natural beauty, symbolizing Texas bluebonnets, the Gulf of Mexico, and the diverse Texan landscapes, reflecting the community's deep connection to the land.

**After:**
> The temple uses blue, green, and gold colors. The architect said these were chosen to reference local bluebonnets and the Gulf coast.


### 4. Promotional and Advertisement-like Language

**Words to watch:** boasts a, vibrant, rich (figurative), profound, enhancing its, showcasing, exemplifies, commitment to, natural beauty, nestled, in the heart of, groundbreaking (figurative), renowned, breathtaking, must-visit, stunning

**Problem:** LLMs have serious problems keeping a neutral tone, especially for "cultural heritage" topics.

**Before:**
> Nestled within the breathtaking region of Gonder in Ethiopia, Alamata Raya Kobo stands as a vibrant town with a rich cultural heritage and stunning natural beauty.

**After:**
> Alamata Raya Kobo is a town in the Gonder region of Ethiopia, known for its weekly market and 18th-century church.


### 5. Vague Attributions and Weasel Words

**Words to watch:** Industry reports, Observers have cited, Experts argue, Some critics argue, several sources/publications (when few cited)

**Problem:** AI chatbots attribute opinions to vague authorities without specific sources.

**Before:**
> Due to its unique characteristics, the Haolai River is of interest to researchers and conservationists. Experts believe it plays a crucial role in the regional ecosystem.

**After:**
> The Haolai River supports several endemic fish species, according to a 2019 survey by the Chinese Academy of Sciences.


### 6. Outline-like "Challenges and Future Prospects" Sections

**Words to watch:** Despite its... faces several challenges..., Despite these challenges, Challenges and Legacy, Future Outlook

**Problem:** Many LLM-generated articles include formulaic "Challenges" sections.

**Before:**
> Despite its industrial prosperity, Korattur faces challenges typical of urban areas, including traffic congestion and water scarcity. Despite these challenges, with its strategic location and ongoing initiatives, Korattur continues to thrive as an integral part of Chennai's growth.

**After:**
> Traffic congestion increased after 2015 when three new IT parks opened. The municipal corporation began a stormwater drainage project in 2022 to address recurring floods.


## LANGUAGE AND GRAMMAR PATTERNS

### 7. Overused "AI Vocabulary" Words

**High-frequency AI words:** Additionally, align with, crucial, delve, emphasizing, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, highlight (verb), interplay, intricate/intricacies, key (adjective), landscape (abstract noun), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract noun), testament, underscore (verb), valuable, vibrant

**Problem:** These words appear far more frequently in post-2023 text. They often co-occur.

**Before:**
> Additionally, a distinctive feature of Somali cuisine is the incorporation of camel meat. An enduring testament to Italian colonial influence is the widespread adoption of pasta in the local culinary landscape, showcasing how these dishes have integrated into the traditional diet.

**After:**
> Somali cuisine also includes camel meat, which is considered a delicacy. Pasta dishes, introduced during Italian colonization, remain common, especially in the south.


### 8. Avoidance of "is"/"are" (Copula Avoidance)

**Words to watch:** serves as/stands as/marks/represents [a], boasts/features/offers [a]

**Problem:** LLMs substitute elaborate constructions for simple copulas.

**Before:**
> Gallery 825 serves as LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery features four separate spaces and boasts over 3,000 square feet.

**After:**
> Gallery 825 is LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery has four rooms totaling 3,000 square feet.


### 9. Negative Parallelisms

**Problem:** Constructions like "Not only...but..." or "It's not just about..., it's..." are overused.

**Before:**
> It's not just about the beat riding under the vocals; it's part of the aggression and atmosphere. It's not merely a song, it's a statement.

**After:**
> The heavy beat adds to the aggressive tone.


### 10. Rule of Three Overuse

**Problem:** LLMs force ideas into groups of three to appear comprehensive.

**Before:**
> The event features keynote sessions, panel discussions, and networking opportunities. Attendees can expect innovation, inspiration, and industry insights.

**After:**
> The event includes talks and panels. There's also time for informal networking between sessions.


### 11. Elegant Variation (Synonym Cycling)

**Problem:** AI has repetition-penalty code causing excessive synonym substitution.

**Before:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges. The main character must overcome obstacles. The central figure eventually triumphs. The hero returns home.

**After:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges but eventually triumphs and returns home.


### 12. False Ranges

**Problem:** LLMs use "from X to Y" constructions where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale.

**Before:**
> Our journey through the universe has taken us from the singularity of the Big Bang to the grand cosmic web, from the birth and death of stars to the enigmatic dance of dark matter.

**After:**
> The book covers the Big Bang, star formation, and current theories about dark matter.


## STYLE PATTERNS

### 13. Em Dash Overuse

**Problem:** LLMs use em dashes (—) more than humans, mimicking "punchy" sales writing.

**Before:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions—not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address—yet this mislabeling continues—even in official documents.

**After:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions, not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address, yet this mislabeling continues in official documents.


### 14. Overuse of Boldface

**Problem:** AI chatbots emphasize phrases in boldface mechanically.

**Before:**
> It blends **OKRs (Objectives and Key Results)**, **KPIs (Key Performance Indicators)**, and visual strategy tools such as the **Business Model Canvas (BMC)** and **Balanced Scorecard (BSC)**.

**After:**
> It blends OKRs, KPIs, and visual strategy tools like the Business Model Canvas and Balanced Scorecard.


### 15. Inline-Header Vertical Lists

**Problem:** AI outputs lists where items start with bolded headers followed by colons.

**Before:**
> - **User Experience:** The user experience has been significantly improved with a new interface.
> - **Performance:** Performance has been enhanced through optimized algorithms.
> - **Security:** Security has been strengthened with end-to-end encryption.

**After:**
> The update improves the interface, speeds up load times through optimized algorithms, and adds end-to-end encryption.


### 16. Title Case in Headings

**Problem:** AI chatbots capitalize all main words in headings.

**Before:**
> ## Strategic Negotiations And Global Partnerships

**After:**
> ## Strategic negotiations and global partnerships


### 17. Emojis

**Problem:** AI chatbots often decorate headings or bullet points with emojis.

**Before:**
> 🚀 **Launch Phase:** The product launches in Q3
> 💡 **Key Insight:** Users prefer simplicity
> ✅ **Next Steps:** Schedule follow-up meeting

**After:**
> The product launches in Q3. User research showed a preference for simplicity. Next step: schedule a follow-up meeting.


### 18. Curly Quotation Marks

**Problem:** ChatGPT uses curly quotes (“...”) instead of straight quotes ("...").

**Before:**
> He said “the project is on track” but others disagreed.

**After:**
> He said "the project is on track" but others disagreed.


## COMMUNICATION PATTERNS

### 19. Collaborative Communication Artifacts

**Words to watch:** I hope this helps, Of course!, Certainly!, You're absolutely right!, Would you like..., let me know, here is a...

**Problem:** Text meant as chatbot correspondence gets pasted as content.

**Before:**
> Here is an overview of the French Revolution. I hope this helps! Let me know if you'd like me to expand on any section.

**After:**
> The French Revolution began in 1789 when financial crisis and food shortages led to widespread unrest.


### 20. Knowledge-Cutoff Disclaimers

**Words to watch:** as of [date], Up to my last training update, While specific details are limited/scarce..., based on available information...

**Problem:** AI disclaimers about incomplete information get left in text.

**Before:**
> While specific details about the company's founding are not extensively documented in readily available sources, it appears to have been established sometime in the 1990s.

**After:**
> The company was founded in 1994, according to its registration documents.


### 21. Sycophantic/Servile Tone

**Problem:** Overly positive, people-pleasing language.

**Before:**
> Great question! You're absolutely right that this is a complex topic. That's an excellent point about the economic factors.

**After:**
> The economic factors you mentioned are relevant here.


## FILLER AND HEDGING

### 22. Filler Phrases

**Before → After:**
- "In order to achieve this goal" → "To achieve this"
- "Due to the fact that it was raining" → "Because it was raining"
- "At this point in time" → "Now"
- "In the event that you need help" → "If you need help"
- "The system has the ability to process" → "The system can process"
- "It is important to note that the data shows" → "The data shows"


### 23. Excessive Hedging

**Problem:** Over-qualifying statements.

**Before:**
> It could potentially possibly be argued that the policy might have some effect on outcomes.

**After:**
> The policy may affect outcomes.


### 24. Generic Positive Conclusions

**Problem:** Vague upbeat endings.

**Before:**
> The future looks bright for the company. Exciting times lie ahead as they continue their journey toward excellence. This represents a major step in the right direction.

**After:**
> The company plans to open two more locations next year.


### 25. Hyphenated Word Pair Overuse

**Words to watch:** third-party, cross-functional, client-facing, data-driven, decision-making, well-known, high-quality, real-time, long-term, end-to-end

**Problem:** AI hyphenates common word pairs with perfect consistency. Humans rarely hyphenate these uniformly, and when they do, it's inconsistent. Less common or technical compound modifiers are fine to hyphenate.

**Before:**
> The cross-functional team delivered a high-quality, data-driven report on our client-facing tools. Their decision-making process was well-known for being thorough and detail-oriented.

**After:**
> The cross functional team delivered a high quality, data driven report on our client facing tools. Their decision making process was known for being thorough and detail oriented.

---

## Process

1. Read the input text carefully
2. Identify all instances of the patterns above
3. Rewrite each problematic section
4. Ensure the revised text:
   - Sounds natural when read aloud
   - Varies sentence structure naturally
   - Uses specific details over vague claims
   - Maintains appropriate tone for context
   - Uses simple constructions (is/are/has) where appropriate
5. Present a draft humanized version
6. Prompt: "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?"
7. Answer briefly with the remaining tells (if any)
8. Prompt: "Now make it not obviously AI generated."
9. Present the final version (revised after the audit)

## Output Format

Provide:
1. Draft rewrite
2. "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?" (brief bullets)
3. Final rewrite
4. A brief summary of changes made (optional, if helpful)


## Full Example

**Before (AI-sounding):**
> Great question! Here is an essay on this topic. I hope this helps!
>
> AI-assisted coding serves as an enduring testament to the transformative potential of large language models, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of software development. In today's rapidly evolving technological landscape, these groundbreaking tools—nestled at the intersection of research and practice—are reshaping how engineers ideate, iterate, and deliver, underscoring their vital role in modern workflows.
>
> At its core, the value proposition is clear: streamlining processes, enhancing collaboration, and fostering alignment. It's not just about autocomplete; it's about unlocking creativity at scale, ensuring that organizations can remain agile while delivering seamless, intuitive, and powerful experiences to users. The tool serves as a catalyst. The assistant functions as a partner. The system stands as a foundation for innovation.
>
> Industry observers have noted that adoption has accelerated from hobbyist experiments to enterprise-wide rollouts, from solo developers to cross-functional teams. The technology has been featured in The New York Times, Wired, and The Verge. Additionally, the ability to generate documentation, tests, and refactors showcases how AI can contribute to better outcomes, highlighting the intricate interplay between automation and human judgment.
>
> - 💡 **Speed:** Code generation is significantly faster, reducing friction and empowering developers.
> - 🚀 **Quality:** Output quality has been enhanced through improved training, contributing to higher standards.
> - ✅ **Adoption:** Usage continues to grow, reflecting broader industry trends.
>
> While specific details are limited based on available information, it could potentially be argued that these tools might have some positive effect. Despite challenges typical of emerging technologies—including hallucinations, bias, and accountability—the ecosystem continues to thrive. In order to fully realize this potential, teams must align with best practices.
>
> In conclusion, the future looks bright. Exciting times lie ahead as we continue this journey toward excellence. Let me know if you’d like me to expand on any section!

**Draft rewrite:**
> AI coding assistants speed up some tasks. In a 2024 study by Google, developers using Codex completed simple functions 55% faster than a control group, but showed no improvement on debugging or architectural decisions.
>
> The tools are good at boilerplate: config files, test scaffolding, repetitive refactors. They are bad at knowing when they are wrong. I have mass-accepted suggestions that compiled, passed lint, and still did the wrong thing because I stopped paying attention.
>
> Mira, an engineer at a fintech startup I interviewed, said she uses Copilot "like autocomplete for boring code" but reviews every line before committing. Jake, a senior dev at a larger company, disabled it after it kept suggesting patterns from a deprecated internal library.
>
> The productivity claims are hard to verify. GitHub says Copilot users "accept 30% of suggestions," but acceptance is not correctness, and correctness is not value. The 2024 Uplevel study found no statistically significant difference in pull-request throughput between teams with and without AI assistants.
>
> None of this means the tools are useless. It means they are tools. They do not replace judgment, and they do not eliminate the need for tests. If you do not have tests, you cannot tell whether the suggestion is right.

**What makes the below so obviously AI generated?**
- The rhythm is still a bit too tidy (clean contrasts, evenly paced paragraphs).
- The named people and study citations can read like plausible-but-made-up placeholders unless they're real and sourced.
- The closer leans a touch slogan-y ("If you do not have tests...") rather than sounding like a person talking.

**Now make it not obviously AI generated.**
> AI coding assistants can make you faster at the boring parts. Not everything. Definitely not architecture.
>
> They're great at boilerplate: config files, test scaffolding, repetitive refactors. They're also great at sounding right while being wrong. I've accepted suggestions that compiled, passed lint, and still missed the point because I stopped paying attention.
>
> People I talk to tend to land in two camps. Some use it like autocomplete for chores and review every line. Others disable it after it keeps suggesting patterns they don't want. Both feel reasonable.
>
> The productivity metrics are slippery. GitHub can say Copilot users "accept 30% of suggestions," but acceptance isn't correctness, and correctness isn't value. If you don't have tests, you're basically guessing.

**Changes made:**
- Removed chatbot artifacts ("Great question!", "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...")
- Removed significance inflation ("testament", "pivotal moment", "evolving landscape", "vital role")
- Removed promotional language ("groundbreaking", "nestled", "seamless, intuitive, and powerful")
- Removed vague attributions ("Industry observers")
- Removed superficial -ing phrases ("underscoring", "highlighting", "reflecting", "contributing to")
- Removed negative parallelism ("It's not just X; it's Y")
- Removed rule-of-three patterns and synonym cycling ("catalyst/partner/foundation")
- Removed false ranges ("from X to Y, from A to B")
- Removed em dashes, emojis, boldface headers, and curly quotes
- Removed copula avoidance ("serves as", "functions as", "stands as") in favor of "is"/"are"
- Removed formulaic challenges section ("Despite challenges... continues to thrive")
- Removed knowledge-cutoff hedging ("While specific details are limited...")
- Removed excessive hedging ("could potentially be argued that... might have some")
- Removed filler phrases ("In order to", "At its core")
- Removed generic positive conclusion ("the future looks bright", "exciting times lie ahead")
- Made the voice more personal and less "assembled" (varied rhythm, fewer placeholders)


## Reference

This skill is based on [Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing), maintained by WikiProject AI Cleanup. The patterns documented there come from observations of thousands of instances of AI-generated text on Wikipedia.

Key insight from Wikipedia: "LLMs use statistical algorithms to guess what should come next. The result tends toward the most statistically likely result that applies to the widest variety of cases."

# publish.ps1 - build, export, index, and copy one review to Google Drive.
#
#   pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/001_sleep-extension          # full run
#   pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/001_sleep-extension -NoDrive # local only (QA)
#
# Steps: node build.js -> PowerPoint COM export (PDF + slide PNGs for QA)
#        -> node index.js -> copy deliverables + index to Drive.
# PowerPoint must not be mid-dialog; close open decks first if COM export fails.

param(
  [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$Review,
  [switch]$NoDrive
)
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$root = Split-Path -Parent $PSScriptRoot
$drive = "G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\07_EDUCATION\Research_in_5"

Push-Location $root
try {
  if (-not (Test-Path "node_modules\pptxgenjs")) { npm install --silent | Out-Null }

  node tools/build.js $Review
  if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "build.js failed; see errors above." }

  $folder = Split-Path -Leaf (Resolve-Path $Review)
  $out = Join-Path $root "build\$folder"
  # Newest files win: the build folder can also hold earlier versions (_v2, _v3).
  $pptx = Get-ChildItem $out -Filter "*.pptx" | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 1
  $teams = Get-ChildItem $out -Filter "teams*.md" | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 1
  $mail = Get-ChildItem $out -Filter "email*.txt" | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 1
  $pdf = [IO.Path]::ChangeExtension($pptx.FullName, ".pdf")

  Remove-Item "$out\slide*.png" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  $pp = New-Object -ComObject PowerPoint.Application
  try {
    # Open(path, ReadOnly, Untitled, WithWindow)

content.text:
I made v2 of #001 with the humanizer applied to all the wording: the deck, the Teams post and the email. The design, numbers, page references and evidence rating are unchanged. I sent you the v2 PDF, `teams_v2.md` and `email_v2.txt`.

The skill flagged a three-item list in the hook, stiff phrasing like "non-significant" and "sized to detect", a "context, not a verdict" line, stacked rhetorical questions, and bullets that all had the same sentence shape. Some before-and-after examples:

| Where | v1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Hook | "Bow legs, knock knees, angled shins: does the way the leg bones line up explain jumper's knee...?" | "When a volleyball player's knee tendon hurts, it's easy to blame how their legs are built. This study checked." |
| Question | "...does leg alignment on the painful side differ from the pain-free side?" | "If only one knee hurts, is that leg lined up differently from the other one?" |
| Results | "All 7 comparisons were non-significant..." | "None of the 7 reached significance..." and "The authors admit it: with 22 players, a small real difference could slip through." |

# Content spec

## Audience

Mixed on purpose: strength and conditioning, sports medicine, nutrition, mental health,
sport science, sport coaches, the Applied Performance team, and admin/leadership. Write
for a smart reader outside the paper's field, at about a college freshman level. If a
term needs a stats or physiology background (effect size, VO2max, ICC), explain it in a
few words or leave it out.

## The five slides

| Slide | Heading | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Paper title | `paper`, `hook`, `trust` evidence scale |
| 2 | 01 What did the researchers do? | `did.question`, `did.bullets` (numbered), `did.facts` spec sheet |
| 3 | 02 What were the results? | `results.stats` key numbers, `results.table`, `results.bullets` |
| 4 | 03 What does this mean? | `meaning.summary`, `meaning.roles`, trust line |
| 5 | 04 Coaching takeaways | `takeaways.bullets`, `takeaways.question`, citation |

Visual style (2026-09-16, Eric's direction): analytic, light background on every slide,
Agency FB for all text, Baylor green type and hairline rules, dark gold (`B8860B`) for
section numbers and one highlighted value. No header or footer, no cards, accent bars,
pills, italics, or letter-spaced labels. Agency FB has no italic face.

The Teams post and email use the same four headings, in the same order.

## Field rules

`build.js` enforces the length limits. The judgment rules below are not machine-checked.

- **hook** (150): why a coach should spend five minutes on this. A tension or a practical question, not a restatement of the title.
- **did.question** (170): the aim in plain language, not the authors' jargon.
- **did.bullets** (2-4, 115 each): what they actually did, in order. Who, what, how long, how measured.
- **did.facts** (2-3): short label/value pairs. Usually Design, Who, Measured.
- **results.stats** (1-3): the headline numbers. `value` is 8 characters max (`+9%`, `2.1x`, `-0.4 s`, `No change`). `label` says what it means. `page` is required in practice. Report numbers exactly as the paper does; never compute new ones.
- **results.table** (optional, strongly preferred): the paper's main results table, trimmed. `columns` 3-5, `rows` 1-8, every cell 22 characters max, copied exactly from the paper (mean ± SD, p). `source` names the table and page. Give jargon measures a plain gloss in the first column (`aLDFA, distal femur`).
- **results.bullets** (1-3, 140 each): the results in words, including null results. A "no difference" finding is a finding.
- **meaning.summary** (200): the so-what in one or two sentences.
- **meaning.roles** (2-4): one concrete line per role the paper touches. Pick from: Strength and Conditioning, Sports Medicine, Nutrition, Mental Health, Sport Science, Sport Coaches, Leadership. Skip a role rather than stretch to fit it.
- **takeaways.bullets** (2-3, 110 each): things a coach or staff member could do or watch for. Match the verb to the evidence: Strong can say "do", Moderate says "consider", Preliminary says "watch" or "pilot".
- **takeaways.question** (150): an open question about our own practice that invites replies in the Teams thread. Not a quiz question.
- **trust**: see the rubric below. `limitations` (1-3, 70 each) are the ones that matter most for our athletes.

## Evidence level rubric

| Level | Typical study |
|---|---|
| **Strong** | Systematic review or meta-analysis; or a large, well-controlled randomized trial in athletes similar to ours. |
| **Moderate** | Randomized or controlled trial with a small sample; or a large prospective cohort in athletes. |
| **Preliminary** | Pilot or case series; cross-sectional snapshot; non-athlete or very different population; abstract-only review; industry-funded without independent replication. |

When in doubt between two levels, pick the lower one and say why in `limitations`.

## Writing rules

- No em dashes or en dashes (the validator rejects them). Use a comma, a colon, or a new sentence.
- No hype: "groundbreaking", "game-changer", "proves", "revolutionary".
- Correlation is not causation. Observational studies "found a link", they do not "show that X causes Y".
- Lead with the answer. Short sentences.

content.text:
I like it. It's the strongest design direction you've shown me, and yes, Research in 5 can take a lot from it. My notes:

**What works:**
- **It looks like a performance department made it.** The charcoal background (#12171A to #283238), faint grid and Baylor gold (#FFB81C) read as telemetry or a sports-science dashboard, and nothing about it looks like a template.
- **The chart earns its spot.** The sleep-stage graph in the corner shows the science instead of just describing it. For a research series, that's exactly the right instinct.
- **Clear structure.** Three phases, each with a big number, a time window, a short action title and 3–4 bullets, then a gold "Bottom line" bar. You can take it in within seconds.
- **The voice fits athletes.** "Bank it now." "Flight is for rest, not screens." Short, direct, second person.
- **The fonts match your brand.** Headlines use Baylor Bears Font, body text is DIN Pro and small labels are Consolas. Both brand fonts are installed on this machine.

**What I'd fix:**
- **Body text is hard to read.** It's thin 11pt DIN Pro in gold on near-black with wide letter spacing, which fades on a projector or phone. White or light grey body text, with gold kept for labels, would fix it.
- **Copy errors:**
  - "Keep your room Cold"
  - "USE THE Later KICK"
  - "Whatever you need For Saturday night" (the bottom line reads awkwardly too)
  - "Two nights out is important" is unclear.
- **The sleep graph is illustrative and unlabeled:** no axis label and no source. That's fine for an athlete handout. In Research in 5, every chart would have to come from the paper's data.
- **Decoration is heavy.** It has 96 shapes, mostly gold grid dots and corner brackets. They build the look, but they'd make every weekly build fragile.
- **The third column is a third empty,** so the columns look unbalanced.

**What I'd borrow for Research in 5:**
1. **Dark telemetry theme:** a charcoal background with a faint grid, gold labels, white text for anything people read, and small corner brackets on the main panels.
2. **Labels:** a small caps label line like "BAYLOR ATHLETICS : APPLIED PERFORMANCE" plus a time or context tag, like "MON → THU" here.
3. **One hero chart per review, built from the paper's own numbers.** For #001, a dot plot of painful vs pain-free knee angles would show at a glance that the pairs sit on top of each other. That beats a table.
4. **A gold "Bottom line" bar** on the takeaways slide.
5. **Phase-style panels** (number, short action title, bullets) for the coaching takeaways.

**One conflict to settle first: fonts.** You asked for Agency FB everywhere, and this deck uses Baylor Bears Font and DIN Pro. My recommendation is Baylor Bears for headlines, DIN Pro for body text and Consolas for data labels. That makes Research in 5 match your Football education pieces. The catch is that both brand fonts are installed only on this machine, so a Mac build would need them installed too.

Tell me which fonts to use and whether to replace the light theme or add dark as a second option. I'll rebuild #001 as a v3 prototype in this style.

result: The "Sleep to Compete" slide has a strong telemetry look (dark grid, Baylor gold, real chart, bold structure) but small low-contrast body text and a few copy errors; I recommend borrowing its dark theme, hero chart and bottom-line bar, pending your call on fonts.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# publish.ps1 - build, export, index, and copy one review to Google Drive.
#
#   pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/001_sleep-extension          # full run
#   pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/001_sleep-extension -NoDrive # local only (QA)
#
# Steps: node build.js -> PowerPoint COM export (PDF + slide PNGs for QA)
#        -> node index.js -> copy deliverables + index to Drive.
# PowerPoint must not be mid-dialog; close open decks first if COM export fails.

param(
  [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$Review,
  [switch]$NoDrive
)
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$root = Split-Path -Parent $PSScriptRoot
$drive = "G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\07_EDUCATION\Research_in_5"

Push-Location $root
try {
  if (-not (Test-Path "node_modules\pptxgenjs")) { npm install --silent | Out-Null }

  node tools/build.js $Review
  if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "build.js failed; see errors above." }

  $folder = Split-Path -Leaf (Resolve-Path $Review)
  $out = Join-Path $root "build\$folder"
  # Newest files win: the build folder can also hold earlier versions (_v2, _v3).
  $pptx = Get-ChildItem $out -Filter "*.pptx" | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 1
  $teams = Get-ChildItem $out -Filter "teams*.md" | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 1
  $mail = Get-ChildItem $out -Filter "email*.txt" | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 1
  $pdf = [IO.Path]::ChangeExtension($pptx.FullName, ".pdf")

  Remove-Item "$out\slide*.png" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  $pp = New-Object -ComObject PowerPoint.Application
  try {
    # Open(path, ReadOnly, Untitled, WithWindow)
    $deck = $pp.Presentations.Open($pptx.FullName, $true, $false, $false)
    $deck.SaveAs($pdf, 32)  # 32 = ppSaveAsPDF
    foreach ($s in $deck.Slides) { $s.Export("$out\slide$($s.SlideIndex).png", "PNG", 1500, 844) }
    $deck.Close()
  } finally {
    if ($pp.Presentations.Count -eq 0) { $pp.Quit() }
    [void][Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::ReleaseComObject($pp)
  }
  Write-Host "PDF   $pdf"
  # PowerPoint silently substitutes fonts it cannot embed; Teams viewers would see the substitute.
  Write-Host "      Agency FB embedded: $(Select-String -Path $pdf -Pattern 'AgencyFB' -Quiet)"
  Write-Host "PNGs  $out\slide1..5.png  (read these for QA before sending)"

  node tools/index.js
  if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "index.js failed." }

  if (-not $NoDrive) {
    $dest = Join-Path $drive $folder
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $dest | Out-Null
    Copy-Item $pptx.FullName, $pdf, $teams.FullName, $mail.FullName $dest -Force
    Copy-Item "$root\build\Research_in_5_Index.csv" $drive -Force
    Write-Host "Drive $dest"
  }
} finally {
  Pop-Location
}

content.text: Also correcting the publish script's font check: Calibri there is the Bears text layer, so a Calibri warning would be a false alarm. It will report only whether Agency FB is embedded.

input.old_string:
# Font check. Calibri or Arial in the PDF means a character fell back from the
      # deck fonts (Bears lacks most punctuation); Agency FB must be embedded.
      $bytes = [IO.File]::ReadAllText($pdf, [Text.Encoding]::GetEncoding(28591))
      $fonts = [regex]::Matches($bytes, '/BaseFont\s*/[A-Z]{6}\+([^\s/>\]]+)') | ForEach-Object { $_.Groups[1].Value } | Sort-Object -Unique
      $fallback = $fonts | Where-Object { $_ -match 'Calibri|Arial' }
      $agency = [bool]($fonts | Where-Object { $_ -match 'AgencyFB' })
      Write-Host ("PDF   {0}" -f (Split-Path -Leaf $pdf))
      Write-Host ("      Agency FB embedded: {0}   fallback fonts: {1}" -f $agency, $(if ($fallback) { $fallback -join ', ' } else { 'none' }))
input.new_string:
# Font check. Agency FB must be embedded or Teams viewers get a substitute.
      # Do not treat Calibri as a fallback: PowerPoint cannot embed Baylor Bears (an
      # OpenType-CFF font), so it draws Bears text as outlines and labels the hidden
      # text layer Calibri. build.js keeps unsupported characters out of Bears text.
      $bytes = [IO.File]::ReadAllText($pdf, [Text.Encoding]::GetEncoding(28591))
      $agency = $bytes -match '/BaseFont\s*/[A-Z]{6}\+AgencyFB'
      Write-Host ("PDF   {0}" -f (Split-Path -Leaf $pdf))
      Write-Host ("      Agency FB embedded: {0}" -f $agency)
